blocks.text: How to use this document

This document explains, in plain language and in detail, the analysis of the 2025-26 leaf spectra of white rust in Indian mustard. It follows the order in which the analysis was done: the experiment and data, the validation design, the pre-processing, Objective 1 (which parts of the spectrum respond to the disease), Objective 2 (how well models can detect and grade the disease), the covariate baseline, robustness checks, discussion and conclusions.
Every table and every figure of the report is reproduced here. After each one there is an explanation panel with the same headings, so that each item can be presented in the same way:

items: **What it shows** – the content of the table or figure in one or two sentences.
**How to read it** – the axes, colours, symbols or columns, so that the item can be read without the report.
**What we found** – the numbers that matter, taken from the analysis.
**What it means** – the interpretation: what the result says about white rust, the spectra or the models, and why it matters.
**Say to the chairman** – one or two sentences that summarise the item when presenting it.

blocks.text: Where a method is introduced, a short panel explains **why it was done** and **how it was done** with these data. Each table and figure caption gives its number in the original report (for example "report Figure 4"), so the two documents can be used side by side. The Excel workbook holds every table as an editable sheet, and the seminar slides follow the same order.

FD1805 was selected in one outer fold only and is not part of the final feature set. None of the results or conclusions change.
Executive summary
What was done

In the 2025-26 season, white rust (~~Albugo candida~~) developed naturally on Indian mustard in 48 field plots at IARI, New Delhi. On four dates (11 and 24 February, 3 and 13 March 2026) individual leaves were measured with an ASD FieldSpec spectroradiometer fitted with a contact probe (350–2500 nm), and each measured leaf was scored visually on the 0–9 scale (grades 0, 1, 3, 5, 7, 9). After removing nine spectra from a leaf position that was not part of the design, 2330 leaf spectra remained. The plots formed one fungicide-sprayed healthy block (plots 1–12) and three unsprayed replications (R1–R3, plots 13–48); each block contained three varieties and four sowing dates (D1–D4).

The analysis answered two thesis objectives with these leaf data. **Objective 1** asked which wavelengths, derivatives and vegetation indices change with white rust, and which compact set of features describes the disease. **Objective 2** asked how well a leaf can be (A) detected as diseased, (B) placed in one of the six grades and (C) given a severity score, using six machine-learning methods and five deep-learning networks, including DT-EDNet, the network of the rice-blast study on which the methodology is based.
How it was done

items: All selection and model fitting were tested with **leave-one-replication-out validation**: models were trained on two replications and tested on the third, which they had never seen, so that leaves of one plot never appeared in both training and test.
Spectra were smoothed (Savitzky–Golay), converted to first derivatives and reduced to 5-nm bands; 41 published indices and three red-edge parameters were computed.

Objective 1 followed the DT-EDNet steps: two-band index maps (NDSI, RSI), SHAP-CARS band selection, a three-band White Rust Index, ReliefF index selection and a variance-inflation check, giving an 11-feature **disease-specific feature set**.

Objective 2 compared SVM, random forest, XGBoost, k-nearest neighbours, PLS-DA/PLSR and a dense network (DNN-F1) with four image networks (DT-EDNet, EfficientNet-B0, ResNet18, ConvNeXt V2-Atto) fed with "pseudo-images" of the features.

A **covariate baseline** model that used only crop age, sowing date, variety, growth stage and weather – no spectra – showed how much of the disease level could be predicted from the calendar alone, so that the spectra were credited only with what they add.

blocks.text: What was found

items: **The disease has a clear spectral signature.** Diseased leaves reflect less near-infrared light, more red and more shortwave-infrared light, and the red-edge position moves 7.7 nm towards shorter wavelengths between grade 0 (709.0 nm) and grade 9 (701.3 nm). This agrees with chlorophyll loss, damaged leaf structure and water loss in infected tissue.

**First derivatives carry the strongest signal.** The derivative at 800 nm correlated with the grade at r = 0.62, against 0.46 for the best reflectance band; all 15 wavelengths chosen by SHAP-CARS were derivative bands. The best two-band index was NDSI(795, 805) (R² 0.36).
**Detection is reliable**: the best model (SVM) reached macro-F1 0.792 and AUC 0.897; sensitivity and specificity were both about 0.83.

**Six grades are difficult**: the best model (ConvNeXt V2-Atto) reached macro-F1 0.360 and overall accuracy 0.39, but most errors were one grade away (75% within one grade; quadratic weighted kappa 0.633). Neighbouring grades overlap spectrally and in visual scoring.
**The severity score is predicted with R² 0.459** (XGBoost; RMSE 2.04 grades); predictions follow the right order but are pulled towards the middle of the scale.

**Machine learning and deep learning performed alike**: differences between the best models were smaller than the fold-to-fold variation. DT-EDNet did not outperform the other networks at leaf level, because 10–16 features give no real image for its attention modules to use.

**The calendar explains much of the epidemic**, but the spectra add real information about severity: beyond the covariate-only model, the spectra raised six-grade macro-F1 by 0.043 and the score R² by 0.083 (both confirmed with plot-level bootstrap intervals).
**The models transfer across varieties and sowing dates** (held-out variety or sowing date performed close to the cross-validated value).

blocks.text: What it means

Leaf spectra can tell a diseased leaf from a healthy one with good reliability and can rank leaves by severity, but they cannot separate all six visual grades. For the UAV phase (2026-27) this supports (i) sensors covering the red edge, the near-infrared shoulder and the shortwave infrared, (ii) keeping derivative features, (iii) reporting detection plus a severity score or a small number of classes, and (iv) always comparing against a covariate baseline. Objective 3 (pre-symptomatic detection) could not be addressed with the 2025-26 data, because no pre-symptomatic dates were sampled.
Key ideas in plain language
Eight ideas from statistics and machine learning are used throughout the analysis. They are explained here once, without formulas, so that the later chapters can be read easily.
Training and testing

A model learns from one part of the data (training) and is judged on another part it has never seen (testing). Only the test result says how well the model would work on new leaves; the training result is always too optimistic.
Over-fitting

A flexible model can memorise the training data, including its noise, instead of learning the general pattern. It then looks excellent on training data and poor on new data. Simple models, feature selection, early stopping and honest testing protect against it.
Cross-validation and blocking

Instead of one split, the data are split several times so that every leaf is tested once. When samples are grouped (leaves within plots), whole groups must stay together in training or test – otherwise the model recognises the group, not the disease. Here whole replications were held out.
Nested selection

Any choice made with the data – which wavelengths, which features, which settings – is itself a kind of training. It must be made using only the training part, otherwise the test result is inflated ("selection bias"). Here every choice was repeated inside each training part.
Class imbalance

When some classes are rare (grade 9 = 6% of leaves), a model can score well by ignoring them. Class weights make errors on rare classes count more, and macro-F1 gives every class equal weight in the evaluation.
Correlation is not the whole story

A feature can correlate with the grade only because both follow time (date, crop age). This is called confounding. The covariate baseline measures how much the calendar alone predicts, so that the spectra are credited only with what they add.
Uncertainty

Every result would change a little with another replication. The spread across the three folds (± SD) and bootstrap confidence intervals show how large that variation is; differences smaller than it should not be called real.
Interpretability

A good model should use the inputs in a way that makes physical sense. SHAP values show which features drive each prediction and in which direction, so that the model can be checked against plant physiology.

blocks.label: Why these ideas matter for this analysis.
blocks.text: Leaf-level disease data are small, grouped by plot, unbalanced across grades and strongly tied to the calendar. Each of these features can make a model look better than it is. The design of this analysis – blocked and nested validation, class weights, macro-F1, the covariate baseline and SHAP – addresses each of them, which is why the reported numbers can be presented with confidence.
How to read the chart types used
Eight kinds of chart appear in this document. A one-paragraph guide to each saves explanation during the presentation.
Mean spectrum with SD band

A line for the average reflectance of a group at every wavelength, with a shaded band of ± 1 standard deviation. Where the bands of two groups overlap, individual leaves of the two groups can look the same even if their averages differ.
Correlation curve
For each wavelength, the correlation r between a spectral value and the grade (−1 to +1). Peaks show where the spectrum follows the disease most closely; the sign shows the direction.
Band-pair (R²) map
A square in which every point is a combination of two wavelengths, coloured by how well an index made from them predicts the grade. Bright areas are useful band combinations.
Box plot and violin plot

The box covers the middle 50% of values, the line inside is the median, the whiskers show the spread; a violin adds the shape of the distribution. Boxes that overlap mean the groups are hard to separate.
Confusion matrix
A table with the true class in rows and the predicted class in columns. The diagonal holds the correct predictions; cells next to the diagonal are near-misses; distant cells are gross errors.
ROC curve

Sensitivity plotted against the false-alarm rate for every possible decision threshold. A curve hugging the upper-left corner is good; the diagonal is chance. The area under it (AUC) summarises it in one number.
Radar (spider) chart
Several metrics on axes radiating from a centre; each model is a polygon. Bigger polygons are better, and the shape shows where a model is strong or weak.
Forest (interval) plot
Points with horizontal bars for an estimate and its 95% confidence interval. If the bar does not cross zero, the effect or gain is statistically clear.

blocks.text: 1. Background and objectives
1.1 White rust and why it needs objective measurement

White rust, caused by the oomycete ~~Albugo candida~~, is one of the most important foliar diseases of Indian mustard (~~Brassica juncea~~). On the lower leaf surface it forms white, blister-like pustules; on the upper surface the infected area becomes chlorotic and later necrotic. Systemic infection deforms the inflorescence into "stag heads" and reduces yield (Saharan et al., 2014; Mishra et al., 2009). Epidemics are favoured by cool, humid weather, typically in December and January in north India (Chattopadhyay et al., 2011).

The disease is normally scored by eye on a 0–9 scale. Visual scoring is quick, but it is subjective, and raters disagree most between neighbouring grades (Bock et al., 2010). Hyperspectral reflectance responds to the changes a pathogen causes inside the leaf – loss of chlorophyll, damage to cell structure and loss of water – and can therefore give an objective, non-destructive measure (Mahlein, 2016; Thomas et al., 2018).
1.2 Why start at leaf level

A contact probe touches the leaf and has its own halogen lamp, so the measured spectrum contains only the leaf: no soil, no shadow, no sky and no atmosphere. Leaf spectra therefore show the pure disease signal that a sensor on an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) will later have to detect inside a mixed canopy pixel (Mahlein et al., 2013; Meng et al., 2020). If the signal is weak at leaf level, it will be weaker from the air; if it is clear, the leaf analysis tells which wavelengths and features the UAV analysis should look for.

blocks.label: In simple words.
blocks.text: The leaf study is the "laboratory version" of the UAV study: it tells us whether white rust can be seen in the spectrum at all, where in the spectrum it is seen, and how finely the severity can be measured when nothing else disturbs the signal.

blocks.text: 2. The experiment and the data
2.1 Field layout and treatments

The 2025-26 experiment had 48 plots of 5 m × 3.5 m, separated by 0.5-m bunds and 2-m channels, in a field of 48 m × 24 m. Plots 1–12 formed the **healthy block**: they were sprayed with fungicide and stayed free of white rust. Plots 13–24, 25–36 and 37–48 were the three **unsprayed replications** (R3, R2 and R1), left to natural infection. No artificial inoculation was made; the disease came from the natural inoculum of the season.

Every block held the same 12 treatment combinations: three varieties (V1, V2, V3) × four sowing dates (D1–D4). The four sowing dates gave crops of four different ages when the epidemic developed at the end of January 2026 (Table below). This is useful: it shows how crop age during the epidemic affects the disease, and it makes the data more varied than a single sowing would.

rows: Crop age at the four sampling dates (DAS)
blocks.caption: Sowing timings (treatments D1–D4 = 50, 40, 30 and 20 days after sowing) and crop age at the four sampling dates (natural infection). (report Table 2)

parts: What it shows
The four sowing dates, the crop age they represent at the end of January 2026, and the crop age of each sowing at the four leaf-sampling dates.
How to read it

Each row is one sowing timing. "Treatment crop age" is the age that defines the treatment (50, 40, 30, 20 days after sowing, DAS); the last column gives the age at 11 Feb, 24 Feb, 3 Mar and 13 Mar 2026.
What we found
At the time of sampling the crops ranged from 33 DAS (D4 on 11 February) to 94 DAS (D1 on 13 March). D1 was always the oldest crop and D4 the youngest.
What it means

Crop age at sampling is the natural time variable of this experiment. Because the disease increases with time, any model must be checked for whether it only learns crop age (or date) instead of the leaf signal – this is why the covariate baseline (Chapter 6.5) was built.
Say to the chairman
"Four sowing dates gave four crop ages under the same natural epidemic; crop age at sampling ran from 33 to 94 days."

blocks.label: Why natural infection matters for the analysis.
blocks.text: With natural infection there is no inoculation date, so time is measured from sowing (days after sowing). All unsprayed plots received the same inoculum and weather; differences between them come from crop age, variety and chance. The healthy block shows what a disease-free leaf of the same age looks like.
2.2 Measuring the leaf spectra and scoring the leaves

On each of the four sampling dates, leaves were measured in all 48 plots with the ASD FieldSpec spectroradiometer fitted with the contact probe and leaf clip. The probe has its own halogen lamp, so the readings do not depend on the sun, clouds or time of day (Milton et al., 2009). Reflectance was recorded from 350 to 2500 nm at 1-nm steps; the files were already corrected for the small jumps at the joins of the three detectors ("splice correction").

Three leaf positions were sampled: the third (L3) and fifth (L5) fully expanded leaf from the top and the lowest green leaf (LL). Each measured leaf was scored on the 0–9 white rust scale (grades 0, 1, 3, 5, 7, 9). Nine spectra of 11 February were labelled L4, which is not a sampled position; they were removed, leaving **2330 leaf spectra**.

blocks.caption: Leaf spectra by sampling date and leaf position. (report Table 3)

parts: What it shows
How many leaf spectra were recorded on each date and at each leaf position.
How to read it
Rows are dates; L3, L5 and LL are the leaf positions; "Leaves per plot" gives the median and range of leaves measured in one plot on that date.
What we found

The number of leaves rose from 419 on 11 February to 723 on 13 March. The lowest green leaf (LL) was sampled less on the first two dates (54 and 108 leaves) and fully on the last two (216 and 241). Every date covered all 48 plots, with a median of 10–15 leaves per plot.
What it means

The data set is large (2330 leaves) but not perfectly balanced: later dates contribute more leaves, and lower leaves are under-represented on the early dates. This was kept in mind when reading results by date and leaf position (Chapter 8.6).
Say to the chairman
"2330 leaves over four dates and 48 plots, about 10–15 leaves per plot per date."

blocks.caption: Sampling dates, growth stages and disease level of the leaf spectra. (report Table 4)

parts: What it shows
The crop age, growth stages, number of leaves, mean grade and percentage of diseased leaves on each date.
How to read it
"Mean grade" is the average of the leaf grades (0–9); "Diseased leaves (%)" is the share of leaves with grade above 0. The last row pools all dates.
What we found

The disease rose quickly between the first two dates: the mean grade went from 0.67 (11 Feb) to 3.39 (24 Feb), then to 3.51 (3 Mar) and 4.43 (13 Mar). The share of diseased leaves jumped from 44.6% to 83.3% and then stayed at 81–85%. Over all dates, 76.3% of leaves were diseased and the mean grade was 3.26. Vegetative leaves occurred only on the first two dates and pod-formation leaves only on the last two.
What it means

Two points matter for the analysis. First, the epidemic was well developed: most leaves after mid-February were diseased, so the data are rich in disease but contain few healthy leaves from the unsprayed plots after the first date. Second, growth stage and date are tied together, so a difference between stages cannot be separated from a difference between dates.
Caution
The "All" row of the original report showed the crop age as 6–36 (a left-over from an earlier draft); the correct range is 33–94 days after sowing, as shown here.
Say to the chairman
"The epidemic built up between 11 and 24 February; after that more than 80% of leaves were diseased and the mean grade kept rising to 4.4."

blocks.caption: Number of leaves in each severity grade (pooled data). (report Table 5)

parts: What it shows
How the 2330 leaves are distributed over the six grades.
How to read it
The first row gives counts, the second the percentage of all leaves.
What we found
Grade 0 (552 leaves, 23.7%) and grade 5 (533, 22.9%) were the most common; grade 9 was the rarest (132 leaves, 5.7%).
What it means

The classes are unequal. A model that ignored this would favour the common grades and rarely predict grade 9. Therefore every model used **balanced class weights**, and the main metric is **macro-F1**, which gives every grade the same importance regardless of its size.
Say to the chairman
"Grade 9 is rare – only 6% of leaves – so all models were trained with class weights and judged with a metric that treats all grades equally."

blocks.caption: Leaves by (a) sampling date, (b) growth stage, (c) variety and (d) leaf position, coloured by severity grade. (report Figure 2)

parts: What it shows
Four bar charts that split the 2330 leaves by date, growth stage, variety and leaf position; each bar is coloured by grade (dark green = grade 0 to purple = grade 9).
How to read it
The height of a bar is the number of leaves; the coloured segments show how many of them fall in each grade; n above each bar is the total.
What we found
(a) On 11 February the bar is almost all green (grades 0 and 1); from 24 February the orange, red and purple segments (grades 5–9) dominate.
(b) Vegetative leaves are mostly grade 0–1 (mean grade 1.44); flowering (3.48) and pod-formation leaves (4.47) carry most of the severe disease.
(c) The three varieties have similar grade mixtures (mean 3.45, 3.37 and 2.96 for V1, V2, V3).
(d) Disease increases down the plant: mean grade 2.59 (L3), 3.35 (L5) and 4.07 (LL).
What it means

The disease level depends strongly on time (date and stage) and on leaf position, and only a little on variety. The higher disease on lower leaves agrees with the biology of white rust: older, lower leaves stay longer in the humid micro-climate near the ground and were exposed to the inoculum for longer.
Say to the chairman
"Disease rose with date and was highest on the lowest leaves; the varieties differed only slightly."

blocks.text: 2.3 Weather and covariates

Daily weather from 1 December 2025 to 20 March 2026 came from the IARI agro-meteorological observatory: maximum and minimum temperature, rainfall, morning (RH I) and afternoon (RH II) relative humidity, wind, sunshine and evaporation. For each sampling date the seven days before the date were summarised; the window ends the day before sampling, so no weather from the future enters any model ("no look-ahead").

Because infection was natural, the number of **favourable days** was counted from each sowing date to the day before sampling, using the white rust criteria of Chattopadhyay et al. (2011): for leaf infection a maximum temperature of 16–24 °C with morning humidity above 97% and afternoon humidity above 40%; for the staghead phase a maximum temperature of 20–29 °C, minimum above 12 °C and morning humidity above 97%. Leaf-level covariates were crop age (DAS), sowing timing, variety and growth stage (vegetative, flowering, pod formation coded 1–3 following the BBCH ranges; Lancashire et al., 1991).

rows: Favourable leaf days since sowing D1 / D2 / D3 / D4
blocks.caption: Weather covariates of the four sampling dates (7-day windows ending the day before each date; favourable days after Chattopadhyay et al., 2011). (report Table 6)

parts: What it shows
The weather of the seven days before each sampling date and the number of favourable days.
How to read it

T max and T min are the mean daily maximum and minimum temperatures; RH I and RH II are morning and afternoon humidity; "Favourable leaf days since sowing" gives one value for each sowing date (D1 / D2 / D3 / D4).
What we found
The weather warmed and dried during sampling: 7-day T max rose from 23.3 to 34.5 °C and afternoon humidity fell from 50% to 33–36%. Almost no rain fell.
Only one favourable leaf-infection day fell within the 7 days before 11 February and none before the other dates.
Since sowing, D1 and D2 had 17 favourable days, D3 13 and D4 7; no staghead-favourable day occurred.
What it means

The infection happened earlier, during the cool, humid spell of December–January (the last favourable day was 4 February). What was measured in February–March is the expression and spread of that infection as the crop aged, under weather that was becoming unfavourable. The earlier sowings were exposed to more favourable days, which helps explain why D1 and D2 had more disease.
Say to the chairman
"Infection happened in the cool, humid weeks of December and January; during sampling the weather became hot and dry."

blocks.text: 2.4 Data organisation and quality control
Before any analysis, the data were organised and checked in seven steps:

items: **Parsing:** the four Excel files were read and the 2330 leaf columns kept; columns holding plot averages were skipped because the analysis is at leaf level.
**Treatments:** each plot number was joined to the field layout (block, sowing date, variety); the variety written in the files agreed with the layout for all 48 plots.

**Labels:** the grade was taken from the score; for detection a leaf is "diseased" when its grade is above 0. All 378 leaves of the sprayed healthy block were grade 0; 1952 leaves came from the unsprayed plots.
**Leaf positions:** only L3, L5 and LL were kept (the nine L4 spectra were removed).
**Derived fields:** crop age at sampling (DAS) and the growth-stage code.

**Checks:** grades only 0, 1, 3, 5, 7, 9; wavelengths 350–2500 nm at 1 nm; no missing values; reflectance between 0.026 and 0.935; all 48 plots on every date; 3–30 leaves per plot and date (median 15).
**Folds:** every leaf was assigned to the validation fold of its plot (Chapter 3).

blocks.label: Why this matters.
blocks.text: Quality control is the reason the results can be trusted: a wrong variety, a mislabelled leaf position or a corrupted spectrum would silently distort every later step. All checks passed; the only change was the removal of the nine L4 spectra.
2.5 Three prediction tasks

blocks.caption: Prediction tasks. (report Table 7)

parts: What it shows
The three questions the models answer and how each is evaluated.
How to read it
Task A has two classes, task B six ordered classes, task C a number from 0 to 9.
What we found
Detection compares 552 healthy with 1778 diseased leaves; six grades uses all six classes; the score treats the grade as a continuous number.
What it means

The three tasks are three levels of detail. Detection is what a farmer or an early-warning system needs first; six grades follow the visual scale used by pathologists; the score is the most natural output for a sensor, because disease severity is continuous. Each task needs its own metric (Chapter 6.4).
Say to the chairman
"I ask three questions of each model: is the leaf diseased, which of the six grades is it, and what is its severity score?"

blocks.text: 3. Validation design: how the models were tested fairly

The single most important methodological decision is how the data are split into training and test parts. If leaves from the same plot appear in both parts, a model can recognise the plot (its soil, micro-climate, variety and timing) instead of the disease, and the test accuracy is inflated. This is called **leakage**. Spatially blocked cross-validation avoids it by keeping whole blocks out of training (Roberts et al., 2017).

rows: The model is trained on two replications and tested on the third, which it has never seen; repeated three times so that every leaf is tested once.

Leaves of one plot share soil, microclimate and inoculum, so random leaf splits would put near-copies in training and test and inflate accuracy. Blocking by replication avoids this (Roberts et al., 2017). The fungicide-protected healthy plots are rotated so that every test fold has four healthy plots.

Spatially blocked cross-validation (Roberts et al., 2017); nested selection and tuning inside the training part to avoid selection bias (Ambroise and McLachlan, 2002; Varma and Simon, 2006; Cawley and Talbot, 2010).

Fold 1 tests R1 (plots 37–48) + healthy plots 7, 2, 10, 12; fold 2 tests R2 + 5, 8, 4, 1; fold 3 tests R3 + 3, 9, 11, 6. Feature selection, SFFS and grid search use only the training part, with inner GroupKFold(3) by plot.
Pooled test predictions of all 2330 leaves for every model.
Leave-one-date-out was not used because the dates differ in growth stage and disease level (see 2.12 for the transfer tests).

Every leaf is predicted exactly once by a model that never saw its replication. The reported accuracy is therefore an honest estimate of how the method would work on a new replication of the same experiment.

blocks.text: 4. Pre-processing and spectral features
4.1 What a leaf spectrum contains

A reflectance spectrum gives, for every wavelength, the fraction of light that the leaf reflects. Different parts of the spectrum respond to different leaf properties (Jacquemoud and Ustin, 2019; Mahlein, 2016):

items: **Visible, 400–700 nm:** absorbed by chlorophyll and carotenoids; reflectance is low except for a small green peak near 550 nm.

**Red edge, 680–760 nm:** the steep rise from the red absorption to the near-infrared plateau. Its position and slope depend on chlorophyll content and are among the most sensitive indicators of plant stress.
**Near infrared (NIR), 760–1300 nm:** high reflectance caused by scattering at cell walls and air spaces in the mesophyll; it falls when the leaf structure is damaged.
**Shortwave infrared (SWIR), 1300–2500 nm:** controlled mainly by leaf water (absorption bands near 1450 and 1940 nm) and by dry matter; reflectance rises when the leaf loses water.

blocks.label: In simple words.
blocks.text: White rust removes chlorophyll (visible and red edge change), damages the cells around the pustules (NIR changes) and dries the tissue (SWIR changes). A leaf spectrum can therefore "see" the disease in three different ways.
4.2 Smoothing, trimming and the first derivative

rows: Spectral range, smoothing and first derivative

Savitzky–Golay smoothing fits a local polynomial in a moving window; the same fit gives the first derivative, which removes additive offsets and sharpens the red edge (Savitzky and Golay, 1964; Tsai and Philpot, 1998).

Contact-probe spectra are clean, but the detector ends (350–399 nm and 2401–2500 nm) are noisy. Water-absorption regions (1350–1460 and 1790–1960 nm) were kept: the probe uses its own light source, so atmospheric water does not affect them, and they carry leaf-water information.
Savitzky–Golay with the first derivative in rice blast (Ma et al., 2026) and wheat diseases (Huang et al., 2020; Meng et al., 2020); derivative analysis of leaf spectra (Tsai and Philpot, 1998).

Savitzky–Golay window 11 nm, order 2, applied on 350–2500 nm; spectra trimmed to 400–2400 nm; first derivative from the same filter; bands taken every 5 nm (401 reflectance + 401 derivative features).
Smoothed reflectance Rλ and first derivative FDλ (×10^{−3} nm^{−1}) at 5 nm.
The second derivative was not used (agreed rule: it amplifies noise). Standard normal variate and continuum removal were not needed for contact-probe data.

parts: Why it was done
The two ends of the detector range (350–399 nm and 2401–2500 nm) are noisy and were trimmed.
Smoothing removes small random fluctuations without changing the shape of the spectrum.

The first derivative (the slope of the spectrum) removes constant offsets – for example a slightly brighter or thicker leaf – and turns the red edge into a sharp peak whose height and position can be measured.
How it was done
Savitzky–Golay filter with an 11-nm window and a second-order polynomial (Savitzky and Golay, 1964), applied to 350–2500 nm and then trimmed to 400–2400 nm.
First derivative from the same filter, in units of 10^{−3} per nm.
Bands taken every 5 nm: 401 reflectance values (R_{400} … R_{2400}) and 401 derivative values (FD400 … FD2400) per leaf.

The water-absorption regions (1350–1460 and 1790–1960 nm) were **kept**: the probe uses its own lamp and touches the leaf, so there is no atmospheric water in the light path, and these regions carry information on leaf water.
What it means
After this step every leaf is described by 802 numbers. They are highly correlated with their neighbours, which is why the selection steps of Objective 1 are needed.
Say to the chairman
"I smoothed the spectra, kept 400–2400 nm including the water bands, and used both reflectance and its first derivative at 5-nm steps."

blocks.text: 4.3 Vegetation indices

A vegetation index combines two or three bands in a formula designed to respond to one leaf property. Forty-one published indices and three red-edge parameters (44 features) were computed for every leaf from the smoothed 1-nm reflectance. They fall into five groups: greenness/structure indices (NDVI, SR, OSAVI, MTVI2 …), pigment indices (PSSR, SIPI, NPCI, PSRI, ARI, PRI), red-edge indices (CIrededge, NDRE, MTCI, REP, Dr, REarea), water indices (WI, WBI, NDWI, MoistSI, NDII) and disease indices (DWSI-1 to 5, HI, RVSI, RBI, NDBI).

rows: wavelength of maximum FD in 680–760 nm
blocks.caption: Vegetation indices and red-edge parameters computed for every leaf, with Pearson r against the leaf grade (n = 2330). (report Table 11)

parts: What it shows
Every index computed, its formula, the paper that proposed it, and its Pearson correlation r with the leaf grade across all 2330 leaves.
How to read it

r ranges from −1 to +1. A negative r means the index falls as disease increases; a positive r means it rises. |r| above about 0.5 is a strong relationship for single leaves; |r| below 0.2 means the index hardly follows the grade.
What we found
Strongest negative: the Healthy Index HI (−0.54), PSSRb (−0.53), SR, RVI, MSR and PSSRa (−0.51), REP (−0.50) and the NDVI family (−0.48 to −0.49).
Strongest positive: RVSI (+0.56, red-edge vegetation stress index) and ARI (+0.53, anthocyanin reflectance index).
Water indices were moderate (|r| 0.37–0.40); MCARI, TCARI, PSSRc, GNDVI and CIgreen were weak (|r| ≤ 0.16).
What it means

The best single published index explains only about 30% of the variation in grade (r² = 0.54² ≈ 0.29). Indices that contrast red or red-edge with NIR work best, confirming that chlorophyll loss and structural change are the main signals. Green-based indices (GNDVI, CIgreen) respond weakly because the green peak changed little (Table of mean reflectance, Chapter 7.2). No single index is enough, which is why the analysis goes on to select a combination of features.
Say to the chairman
"The best published indices – HI, PSSRb, REP and RVSI – correlate at about |r| = 0.5 with the grade; useful, but no single index is enough."

blocks.text: 5. Objective 1 methods: finding the disease-specific features

Objective 1 follows the steps of the DT-EDNet rice-blast study (Ma et al., 2026). The idea is to go from 802 bands and 44 indices to a small set of features that carry the disease signal and are not redundant. Four activities do this, each summarised in a "step card" from the report.
5.1 Activity 1.1 – Response analysis

rows: Mean reflectance and first-derivative curves of each grade show where and how the spectrum changes with disease; Pearson correlation of each band with the grade measures the strength of the change.
It is the first, model-free evidence of the disease signal and shows whether the response is consistent across varieties, stages and dates.
Mean spectra and correlation curves are the standard first step in disease spectroscopy (Mahlein et al., 2013; Meng et al., 2020; Mandal et al., 2023; Ma et al., 2026).
Means ± SD by grade for 400–2400 nm; first derivative; r of each 5-nm band and derivative with the grade; spectra by growth stage; mean grade by stage, variety, leaf position and timing.
Disease-sensitive regions; evidence for the band selection that follows.

parts: Why it was done
Before any model, the raw evidence: does the spectrum change with disease, where, and in which direction? This is model-free and easy to check.
How it was done

Mean reflectance and mean derivative of each grade (± SD) over 400–2400 nm; Pearson r of every 5-nm band with the grade; mean spectra within each growth stage; mean grade by stage, variety, leaf position and sowing timing.
What it means
These curves are the basis for all later selection steps and for the physical interpretation in the discussion.
Say to the chairman
"First I simply looked at how the average spectrum of each grade differs."

blocks.text: 5.2 Activity 1.2 – Effective ranges and optimal wavelengths (SHAP-CARS)

rows: Activity 1.2 – Effective ranges and optimal wavelengths (SHAP-CARS)

NDSI and RSI are computed for every pair of bands; the R² with the grade forms a map whose high-value area defines the effective wavelength ranges. Inside them, a gradient-boosting model ranks bands by mean |SHAP| (top 40% kept) and CARS with PLS selects the final optimal wavelengths.
802 correlated bands cannot go into a model directly. SHAP removes uninformative bands before CARS, so CARS works on a smaller, relevant set and is more stable (Ma et al., 2026).
NDSI/RSI R² maps and SHAP-CARS for rice blast (Ma et al., 2026); CARS (Li et al., 2009); SHAP (Lundberg and Lee, 2017; Lundberg et al., 2020).

Threshold R² ≥ 0.5 for effective ranges, else the top 5% of pairs (used here: R² ≥ 0.228); red-edge derivatives 680–760 nm always candidates; XGBoost (300 trees, depth 4, learning rate 0.05); bands standardised; PLS components by Monte Carlo cross-validation (50 splits); CARS 50 iterations × 20 runs; bands kept if selected in ≥ 50% of runs (maximum 15).
Reflectance and derivative bands were pooled in one SHAP-CARS run (agreed decision).
blocks.caption: Step card – Activity 1.2 – Effective ranges and optimal wavelengths (SHAP-CARS). (report Table 13)

blocks.text: This activity uses four techniques. Each is explained here in plain terms:

items: **NDSI and RSI maps.** For every pair of bands (λ_{1}, λ_{2}) the normalised difference NDSI = (R_{λ1} − R_{λ2})/(R_{λ1} + R_{λ2}) and the ratio RSI = R_{λ1}/R_{λ2} are computed, and their R² with the grade is drawn as a coloured map. Bright areas show which band combinations follow the disease. The area above a threshold defines the "effective ranges" of wavelengths.

**SHAP (Shapley additive explanations).** A gradient-boosting model (XGBoost) is trained to predict the grade from all candidate bands. SHAP measures how much each band contributes to the predictions, averaged over all leaves (Lundberg and Lee, 2017). Bands in the top 40% of mean |SHAP| are kept; the rest are discarded.

**PLS (partial least squares).** A regression method that compresses many correlated bands into a few "latent components" that best predict the grade. Its number of components was chosen by Monte Carlo cross-validation (50 random splits).

**CARS (competitive adaptive reweighted sampling).** Starting from the SHAP-screened bands, CARS repeatedly fits PLS, removes bands with small PLS coefficients and keeps the subset with the lowest cross-validated error (Li et al., 2009). Running CARS 20 times and keeping bands selected in at least half of the runs (maximum 15) makes the selection stable.

parts: Why it was done

802 correlated bands cannot be given directly to a model: many are redundant and some are noise. SHAP removes uninformative bands first, so that CARS works on a smaller, relevant set and gives a more stable answer (Ma et al., 2026).
How it was done
Threshold for effective ranges: R² ≥ 0.5, or – if no pair reaches it – the top 5% of all pairs (used here: R² ≥ 0.228).
Red-edge derivatives (680–760 nm) were always candidates, because of their known link to chlorophyll.
XGBoost with 300 trees, depth 4, learning rate 0.05; bands standardised; CARS 50 iterations × 20 runs.
What it means
The output is a list of **optimal wavelengths (OW)** – the individual bands that best describe the disease.
Say to the chairman
"Band-pair maps showed where the signal is; SHAP and CARS then picked the 15 most informative bands."

blocks.text: 5.3 Activities 1.3–1.4 – Index construction and ReliefF selection

rows: Activities 1.3–1.4 – Index construction and ReliefF selection

The best NDSI and RSI pairs come from the maps; the White Rust Index adds a third band to the best NDSI: WRI = NDSI(λ1, λ2) + w·Rλ3. Indices with |r| ≥ 0.95 are reduced to the one most correlated with the grade; ReliefF (classes) and RReliefF (score) rank the rest.

A three-band index can correct a confounding effect that a two-band index cannot; ReliefF judges an index by how well it separates near neighbours of different classes, so it handles interactions and is not fooled by correlation alone.

Three-band disease indices (Meng et al., 2020; Mandal et al., 2023; Ma et al., 2026); ReliefF and RReliefF (Kira and Rendell, 1992; Kononenko, 1994; Robnik-Šikonja and Kononenko, 2003; Urbanowicz et al., 2018).

WRI search: the 200 best NDSI pairs at least 50 nm apart, λ3 every 10 nm, w ∈ {−1, −0.5, 0, 0.5, 1}. ReliefF with k = 10 neighbours, neighbours from the same plot excluded; top five indices kept for each task.
Selected indices (VI) for detection, six grades and score.
blocks.caption: Step card – Activities 1.3–1.4 – Index construction and ReliefF selection. (report Table 14)

blocks.text: Three data-driven indices were added to the 44 published features: the best NDSI and RSI from the maps (NDSI_best, RSI_best) and a **White Rust Index (WRI)** that adds a weighted third band to the best two-band index: WRI = NDSI(λ_{1}, λ_{2}) + w·R_{λ3}. A third band can correct an effect that a two-band index cannot, for example leaf thickness. The search tried the 200 best NDSI pairs, every third band at 10-nm steps and five weights (w = −1, −0.5, 0, 0.5, 1).

Indices that were nearly identical (|r| ≥ 0.95 with each other) were reduced to the one most correlated with the grade. The remaining indices were ranked with **ReliefF** (for the classes) and **RReliefF** (for the score). ReliefF looks at each leaf and its nearest neighbours: a good index has similar values for neighbours of the same grade and different values for neighbours of a different grade (Kira and Rendell, 1992; Robnik-Šikonja and Kononenko, 2003). Unlike correlation, it can reward an index that is useful only together with others. Neighbours from the same plot were excluded so that plot similarity could not inflate the weights. The top five indices were kept for each task.

parts: Why it was done
Indices summarise physiology in a form that is easy to interpret and to transfer to other sensors; ReliefF chooses the indices that separate grades among similar leaves.
What it means
The output is the **selected indices (VI)** for detection, six grades and score.
Say to the chairman
"I built a White Rust Index and let ReliefF pick the five most useful indices for each task."

rows: Activity 1.6 – Variance inflation factor and the disease-specific feature set
VIF = 1/(1 − R²j) measures how well feature j is explained by the others; the feature with the largest VIF is removed until all are below 10.
Optimal wavelengths and indices overlap; strong collinearity makes models unstable and explanations unreliable (Dormann et al., 2013; O'Brien, 2007).
VIF screening before modelling (Dormann et al., 2013; Mandal et al., 2023).
Pool = optimal wavelengths + selected indices; iterative removal until all VIF < 10.
Disease-specific feature set (DSF): the input of Objective 2.

blocks.text: Here R_{j}^{2} is the R² obtained when feature j is predicted from all the other features. A VIF of 1 means the feature is independent of the others; a VIF of 10 means 90% of its variation is already contained in the others. The feature with the largest VIF was removed one at a time until all VIFs were below 10 (Dormann et al., 2013).

parts: Why it was done

Optimal wavelengths and indices overlap (several derivative bands near 800–870 nm carry almost the same information). Strongly collinear inputs make models unstable and make explanations (such as SHAP) unreliable.
What it means
The output is the **disease-specific feature set (DSF)**: a compact, non-redundant set of bands and indices that is the main input of Objective 2.
Say to the chairman
"Finally I removed overlapping features until each one carried its own information; the result is an 11-feature disease-specific set."

blocks.label: Important: selection was repeated inside each fold.
blocks.text: For the final description of the signal (Chapter 7) the selection was run once on all leaves. For the models (Chapter 8) the whole selection – maps, SHAP-CARS, ReliefF and VIF – was repeated inside the training part of each outer fold, so the test replication never influenced which features were used.
6. Objective 2 methods: models, metrics and the covariate baseline
6.1 How each model was built inside a fold
Inside every outer training part, the model-building followed the same four steps:

items: **Fold-wise Objective 1:** the effective ranges, SHAP-CARS, the indices, ReliefF and the VIF check were repeated on the training leaves only, giving a disease-specific feature set for that fold and task.

**Sequential floating forward selection (SFFS):** each machine-learning model chose its own compact subset of these features. SFFS adds the feature that improves the inner score most, and after each addition tries removing a feature again ("floating"), which avoids getting stuck with an early poor choice (Pudil et al., 1994). Up to 15 features; the smallest subset within 1% of the best inner score was kept, to favour simple models.
**Grid search:** the model settings (hyper-parameters) were chosen from a small grid by the inner GroupKFold(3) score.
**Standardisation:** every feature was centred and scaled with the mean and SD of the training leaves only, and the same values were applied to the test leaves.

blocks.text: 6.2 The machine-learning models

rows: maximum-margin boundary with radial basis kernel
many decorrelated decision trees, majority vote / mean
label of the nearest training leaves
latent components maximising covariance with the target
Wold et al. (2001); Barker and Rayens (2003)
blocks.caption: Machine-learning models and tuning grids (class weights balanced; SFFS up to 15 features, smallest subset within 1% of the best inner score). (report Table 16)

blocks.text: In plain terms:

items: **Support vector machine (SVM / SVR):** finds the boundary between classes that leaves the widest possible margin; the radial-basis kernel lets the boundary curve. Strong on small, well-chosen feature sets (Cortes and Vapnik, 1995).
**Random forest (RF):** grows 500 decision trees, each on a random sample of leaves and features, and lets them vote (classes) or averages them (score). Robust and hard to over-fit (Breiman, 2001).
**XGBoost:** builds trees one after another, each correcting the errors of the previous ones, with regularisation to control over-fitting (Chen and Guestrin, 2016).
**k-nearest neighbours (k-NN):** gives a leaf the grade most common among its k most similar training leaves. Simple and a useful reference (Cover and Hart, 1967).
**PLS-DA / PLSR:** the classical chemometric method: compresses the features into a few latent components and classifies (DA) or regresses (R) on them (Wold et al., 2001).

parts: What it shows
The five machine-learning methods, their principle, the settings searched, and the original reference.
How to read it
"Grid searched" lists the values tried; the best combination was chosen inside each fold by the inner cross-validation score.
What it means

The set covers the main families: kernel (SVM), bagged trees (RF), boosted trees (XGBoost), instance-based (k-NN) and linear latent-variable models (PLS). Class weights were balanced in all of them, so the rare grade 9 was not ignored.
Say to the chairman
"Five standard machine-learning methods, each tuned and given its own feature subset inside every fold."

DT-EDNet is the network proposed for early rice-blast detection; EfficientNet-B0, ResNet18 and ConvNeXt V2 are the comparison networks of the same study, so the comparison follows the paper.

blocks.text: Five networks were compared:

items: **DNN-F1:** a small fully connected network (about 3000 weights) that takes the feature vector directly – the deep-learning counterpart of the machine-learning models.

**DT-EDNet** (Ma et al., 2026): the network proposed for early rice-blast detection. It embeds the input, re-weights its channels with a squeeze-and-excitation (SE) block, passes it through a dual transformer group (DTG: a kernel transformer block with CBAM attention and four token transformer blocks) and classifies from a class token.
**EfficientNet-B0, ResNet18, ConvNeXt V2-Atto:** well-known image networks used as comparisons in the DT-EDNet paper (Tan and Le, 2019; He et al., 2016; Woo et al., 2023).

blocks.label: What is a "pseudo-image"?
text: Image networks need a grid of pixels. Leaf spectra after selection are a list of 10–16 numbers. The numbers were therefore placed in a k × k grid (k = ⌈√p⌉ = 4 here), with zeros filling the empty cells (Sharma et al., 2019).

Such a 4 × 4 "image" is only an arrangement of features: neighbouring cells are not neighbouring places on a leaf. This is important for understanding why the image networks did not outperform simpler models (Chapter 8.4).

blocks.text: How DT-EDNet processes an input, step by step

items: **Embedding:** a 3 × 3 convolution turns the 4 × 4 input into 128 feature maps – 128 different "views" of the input.
**Squeeze-and-excitation (SE):** the network summarises each of the 128 maps by its average, learns which maps matter, and scales them up or down (Hu et al., 2018).
**Kernel transformer block with CBAM:** an attention block that learns where (spatial attention) and on which maps (channel attention) to concentrate (Woo et al., 2018).

**Four token transformer blocks:** the maps are cut into small "tokens" and a transformer lets every token look at every other token through four attention heads (Vaswani et al., 2017), so relations between distant parts of the input can be learned.
**Class token and output:** a special token collects the information from all others and is turned into the class probabilities (or the score).

blocks.text: Each of these components is designed to find structure in an image – which parts of it matter and how they relate. On a real hyperspectral image of a canopy, that structure exists (lesions, leaves, background); on a 4 × 4 arrangement of features it largely does not. Keeping this in mind explains the ablation results in Chapter 8.4.

parts: Why it was done
DT-EDNet and its comparison networks are part of the thesis methodology; testing them on leaf data shows how they behave before the UAV images are available.
How it was done
Settings of the DT-EDNet paper: AdamW optimiser (learning rate 6 × 10^{−4}, weight decay 10^{−5}), cosine decay, batch 32, label smoothing 0.01, gradient clipping, class-weighted loss.
Up to 100 epochs with early stopping (patience 20) on one third of the training plots used as validation; seed 42; CPU training; no extra tuning.
Stems with stride 1, because a 4 × 4 input would vanish after the usual down-sampling.
Caution
The networks were not tuned separately, so their ranking could change slightly with tuning. DNN-F2 (fusion of several sensors) does not apply to one sensor.
Say to the chairman
"I trained the four image networks of the DT-EDNet paper and a plain dense network with the paper's settings, using the selected features arranged as small pseudo-images."

true-positive rate, true-negative rate, area under the ROC curve (Fawcett, 2006)
kappa with penalty growing with the squared grade distance (Cohen, 1968)
share of leaves predicted at most one class away

blocks.text: The metrics are easiest to understand with a real example. For detection, the best model (SVM) produced the following pooled confusion matrix over the 2330 test leaves:

blocks.caption: Worked example: detection confusion matrix of the SVM (pooled leave-one-replication-out test predictions).

items: **Overall accuracy (OA)** = (460 + 1477) / 2330 = 0.831: 83% of leaves were classified correctly.
**Sensitivity** = 1477 / 1778 = 0.831: 83% of diseased leaves were found. **Specificity** = 460 / 552 = 0.833: 83% of healthy leaves were correctly called healthy.

**F1** of a class combines precision (how many of the leaves called "diseased" really are) and recall (how many diseased leaves were found): F1 = 2PR/(P + R). **Macro-F1** is the simple average of the F1 of all classes, so a small class counts as much as a large one (Sokolova and Lapalme, 2009). For this SVM macro-F1 = 0.792.
**Cohen's kappa** compares the agreement with what chance alone would give: 0 = no better than chance, 1 = perfect (Cohen, 1960). Here 0.587.

**AUC** (area under the ROC curve) is the probability that a randomly chosen diseased leaf receives a higher disease score than a randomly chosen healthy leaf: 0.5 = chance, 1 = perfect (Fawcett, 2006). Here 0.897.

blocks.text: For six grades two further measures matter, because the grades are ordered:

items: **Quadratic weighted kappa (QWK)** gives partial credit: predicting grade 5 for a grade-7 leaf is a small error, predicting grade 0 is a large one; the penalty grows with the square of the distance (Cohen, 1968).
**Within one grade** is the share of leaves predicted in the correct class or a neighbouring one.

blocks.text: For the severity score: **R²** (share of the variation in grade explained by the model), **RMSE** and **MAE** (typical error in grade units), **bias** (average over- or under-prediction) and **RPD** = SD of the observed grades / RMSE. RPD above 2 is usually called good, 1.4–2 fair and below 1.4 poor (Williams, 2001).

parts: What it shows
The definition and purpose of each metric, and which task it is used for.
What it means

No single metric tells the whole story. Macro-F1 is the main metric for classes because the classes are unequal; QWK and "within one grade" are essential for the ordered six grades, because a near-miss is not the same as a gross error; R² and RMSE describe the score in grade units that a pathologist understands.
Say to the chairman
"I report macro-F1 because the classes are unequal, AUC for detection, weighted kappa for the ordered grades, and R² and RMSE in grade units for the score."

blocks.text: 6.5 The covariate baseline: what can be predicted without any spectra?

Severity rose with crop age and date and differed with variety, sowing date, growth stage and weather. A spectral model could therefore look accurate simply by learning the calendar – for example "late date = more disease" – without reading anything from the leaf (De Wolf and Isard, 2007). To guard against this, a model was built that uses **only** the covariates, and the spectra were credited only with what they add to it (Kuhn and Johnson, 2013). Weather-based models can predict disease well (Bijlwan et al., 2025), and adding sensor data to weather data has improved disease forecasts in wheat (Zhang et al., 2014; Ruan et al., 2022).
