parts: What it shows
The three types of covariate-only model fitted for each task and the covariates each one used.
How to read it
B1 is an interpretable statistical model (logistic, ordinal logistic or linear regression); the random forest and "B2" (the best machine-learning model of each task) use all covariates.
What it means

Using an interpretable model alongside flexible ones shows both how well the calendar predicts disease and in which direction each covariate acts. With only four dates the 7-day weather is the same for all leaves of a date, so weather cannot be separated from date; crop age (DAS) and DAS² stand for time in B1.
Say to the chairman
"Before crediting the spectra, I asked how much a model knowing only crop age, sowing date, variety, stage and weather could predict."

items: **Samples:** only the 1952 unsprayed, naturally infected leaves. The healthy block was sprayed and shares every covariate with the unsprayed plots, so including it would teach a false rule.
**Three inputs:** covariates only, leaf spectra only (the fold-wise disease-specific features) and spectra + covariates; same outer folds and inner tuning as before.

**Three gains:** ΔS = spectra model − best covariate model (what the spectra add); ΔC = spectra + covariates − spectra (what the covariates add to the spectra); ΔT = spectra + covariates − covariate model.

**When is a gain real?** A 95% confidence interval was obtained from 2000 bootstrap resamples that resample whole plots (Efron and Tibshirani, 1993). A gain is called real only if the interval excludes zero, the gain is larger than the fold-to-fold SD and it has the same sign in all three folds. AUCs were also compared with the DeLong test (DeLong et al., 1988).

blocks.label: Why this is a strict test.
blocks.text: Requiring all three conditions means a gain is accepted only when it is statistically clear, larger than the normal variation between replications and consistent across all of them. Small or erratic gains are not counted, so the spectra are not over-credited.
6.6 Interpretation and robustness checks

items: **SHAP** of an XGBoost model on the disease-specific features shows the direction and size of each feature's effect (Lundberg and Lee, 2017).
**Strata:** the test metrics of the best models were computed separately for each growth stage, variety, leaf position, date and sowing timing.

**Transfer tests:** a random forest was trained on two varieties and tested on the third (leave-one-variety-out), and trained on three sowing dates and tested on the fourth (leave-one-timing-out), with feature selection repeated inside each training set.
**Selection stability:** how often each optimal wavelength and index was chosen across the three folds.

blocks.text: 6.7 Software and the final models

The analysis used Python 3 with NumPy, pandas, SciPy, scikit-learn (Pedregosa et al., 2011), mlxtend (Raschka, 2018), XGBoost, SHAP and PyTorch (Paszke et al., 2019). After evaluation, every model was refitted once on all 2330 leaves with the same procedure and saved, together with the feature definitions and a prediction script for new spectra (Appendix C). These final models are the ones applied to the UAV images.
7. Results of Objective 1: the spectral signature of white rust
7.1 Disease progress and weather

blocks.caption: Weather of the season with sowing dates, favourable leaf-infection days and the four sampling dates (boxes: mean grade and % diseased leaves); natural infection. (report Figure 3)

parts: What it shows
The whole season from 1 December 2025 to late March 2026: temperature (top), rainfall and humidity (bottom), the four sowing dates and the four sampling dates.
How to read it

Top panel: red line = daily maximum temperature, blue line = minimum; the pale green band marks 16–24 °C (the favourable temperature range); green triangles mark days that met all leaf-infection criteria; dotted green lines are the sowing dates D1–D4; purple lines are the sampling dates, with boxes giving the mean grade and % diseased leaves.
Bottom panel: blue bars = rainfall; dark line = morning humidity (RH I); grey line = afternoon humidity (RH II).
What we found
Favourable days occurred between 18 December and 4 February: 7 in December, 7 in January and 3 in early February (17 in all), several of them around the rain of late January.
Morning humidity stayed near 90–100% through the season; afternoon humidity peaked at 80–95% on a few days in late December and late January.
From mid-February the maximum temperature climbed above 25 °C and reached about 35 °C by mid-March, well above the favourable range.
Disease rose from mean grade 0.7 (44% of leaves diseased) on 11 February to 3.4 (83%) on 24 February and 4.4 (85%) on 13 March.
What it means

The infection was established during the cool, humid spell of December–January, with a last boost from the late-January rain. The rapid rise between 11 and 24 February is the appearance of those infections as symptoms. The later dates show the disease spreading and intensifying on ageing leaves, while the hot, dry weather limited new infection.
Say to the chairman
"The favourable weather came in December and January; what I measured in February and March is that infection becoming visible and intensifying."

blocks.caption: Disease progress and 7-day weather before each sampling date. *Days from the first sowing (9 Dec 2025) to the day before the date with T max 16–24 °C, RH I > 97% and RH II > 40% (Chattopadhyay et al., 2011). (report Table 20)

parts: What it shows
The same story in numbers: crop age, disease level and the 7-day weather before each sampling date, with favourable days counted from the first sowing.
What we found

Mean grade 0.67 → 3.39 → 3.51 → 4.43; diseased 45% → 83% → 81% → 85%; 7-day T max 23.3 → 34.5 °C; afternoon humidity 50% → 36%. The count of favourable days since the first sowing stays at 17 for all dates, because no favourable day fell in the sampling period.
What it means

The weather during sampling cannot explain the differences between dates: it was unfavourable throughout. With only four dates, the weather is identical for all leaves of a date and therefore cannot be tested as a separate predictor in this season; the 13 flights of 2026-27 will allow that.
Say to the chairman
"During sampling it was getting hotter and drier; the disease I measured reflects infection that took place earlier."

blocks.text: 7.2 How the spectrum changes with disease

blocks.caption: (a) Mean leaf reflectance (± SD) of each severity grade over 400–2400 nm (water bands shaded and kept); (b) first derivative at the red edge. (report Figure 4)

parts: What it shows
(a) The average reflectance spectrum of each grade with its spread; (b) a close-up of the first derivative between 500 and 800 nm.
How to read it
Each line is the mean of all leaves of one grade (dark green = grade 0, purple = grade 9); the shaded band around each line is ± 1 SD. Blue shading marks the water-absorption regions.
Labels at the top mark the regions: VIS (visible), RE (red edge), NIR, SWIR-1 and SWIR-2.
In (b) the tall peak near 700–720 nm is the red edge: its height is Dr and its wavelength is REP.
What we found
NIR plateau (750–1300 nm): grades 0 and 1 are highest (about 0.61 at 800 nm); the higher grades are lower (0.55–0.58).
Red (around 680 nm): reflectance rises with grade, so the red trough becomes shallower.
SWIR and water bands: reflectance rises with grade, most clearly in the water bands near 1450 and 1940 nm.
(b) The red-edge peak becomes lower and moves to shorter wavelengths as grade increases.
The SD bands overlap widely: individual leaves of different grades can have very similar spectra.
What it means

All three expected effects of white rust are visible: chlorophyll loss (red and red edge), structural damage (NIR) and water loss (SWIR). The large overlap of the SD bands is the first warning that individual leaves of neighbouring grades will be hard to separate.
Say to the chairman
"Diseased leaves reflect less near-infrared, more red and more shortwave-infrared light, and the red edge shifts towards shorter wavelengths."

blocks.caption: Mean reflectance at key wavelengths and red-edge parameters by grade. (report Table 21)

parts: What it shows
The mean reflectance of each grade at nine key wavelengths and the two red-edge parameters, with the change from grade 0 to grade 9.
How to read it
The last column gives the percentage change between grade 0 and grade 9 (for REP, the change in nm).
What we found
Largest relative increases: 1940 nm water band (+66%), 1450 nm water band (+49%), 680 nm red (+45%) and 2200 nm (+34%).
Decreases: 760 nm (−11%) and 800 nm (−9.5%) on the NIR plateau; Dr −16%.
REP falls from 709.0 nm (grade 0) to 701.3 nm (grade 9): a blue shift of 7.7 nm, almost step by step (708.5, 705.2, 703.5, 701.8 nm for grades 1–7).
The green band (550 nm) hardly changes (+6%).
What it means

The red-edge position is the most regular indicator: it moves monotonically with grade. The water bands show the largest relative change, which supports keeping them in the analysis of contact-probe data. A blue shift of this size (about 8 nm) is typical of chlorophyll loss in diseased leaves (Mahlein et al., 2013; Meng et al., 2020).
Say to the chairman
"The red-edge position moves 7.7 nm from 709 to 701 nm between healthy and grade-9 leaves, and the water bands change by 50–66%."

blocks.caption: First derivative of the mean spectra of each grade over 400–2400 nm. (report Figure 5)

parts: What it shows
The slope of the mean spectrum of each grade across the full range.
How to read it
Positive values mean reflectance is rising with wavelength, negative values that it is falling. Peaks mark the steepest parts of the spectrum.
What we found
The red-edge peak near 720 nm is by far the largest and is lower for higher grades.
Smaller differences appear at the green peak (around 520–570 nm), at the edges of the water bands (near 1380, 1450, 1870 nm) and in the SWIR-2.
What it means

The derivative turns small changes of shape into visible peaks. It shows that the disease signal is not only in the red edge: the flanks of the water bands also respond, which is why derivative bands from the NIR and SWIR are selected later.
Say to the chairman
"The derivative makes the red edge and the water-band edges stand out; both respond to the disease."

blocks.caption: Mean reflectance by grade within each growth stage. (report Figure 6)

parts: What it shows
The mean spectra of each grade drawn separately for the vegetative, flowering and pod-formation stages.
How to read it
Compare the lines within one panel (the grade effect at a given stage) and between panels (the stage effect).
What we found
Vegetative (n = 555): the grade lines almost coincide; these leaves are mostly grade 0–1, so there is little disease to see.
Flowering (n = 1160): a clear grade effect – NIR falls and SWIR rises with grade.
Pod formation (n = 615): SWIR and the water bands rise strongly with grade; on the NIR plateau the higher grades are slightly **higher**, the opposite of flowering.
What it means

The SWIR/water-band increase is consistent wherever there is disease, but the direction of the NIR change depends on the stage. This is an important caution: NIR reflectance on its own is not a stable disease indicator, because leaf ageing and canopy development also change it. Indicators based on the red edge and the water bands are more robust.
Caution
Growth stage and date are linked in this design (vegetative leaves only on the first two dates, pod formation only on the last two), so stage effects cannot be separated from date effects.
Say to the chairman
"The water-band signal is present at every stage with disease; the near-infrared change depends on the stage, so it is not a reliable indicator on its own."

blocks.caption: Mean leaf grade (± 95% confidence interval) by growth stage, variety, leaf position and sowing timing. (report Figure 7)

parts: What it shows
The average grade in each level of four factors, with 95% confidence intervals.
How to read it
Bar height = mean grade; the error bar = 95% confidence interval; n = number of leaves. Non-overlapping error bars indicate a clear difference.
What we found
Growth stage: vegetative 1.44, flowering 3.48, pod formation 4.47.
Variety: V1 3.45, V2 3.37, V3 2.96 – V3 had somewhat less disease.
Leaf position: L3 2.59, L5 3.35, LL 4.07 – disease increases down the plant.
What it means

The large stage differences mostly reflect the date (later dates = later stages = more disease). Leaf position is a genuine within-date effect: the lower leaves carry more disease. The variety and timing differences are smaller; the covariate model (Chapter 8.8) shows that, at the same crop age, the late sowing D4 actually had more disease.
Say to the chairman
"Disease increased with stage and down the plant; V3 had the least disease."

blocks.caption: Pearson correlation of reflectance and first derivative with the leaf grade (dotted lines: |r| = 0.3). (report Figure 8)

parts: What it shows
For every wavelength, how strongly reflectance (blue) and its first derivative (red) follow the grade across all 2330 leaves.
How to read it

The curve gives r at each wavelength; above zero means the value rises with grade, below zero that it falls. Dotted lines at ±0.3 mark a moderate correlation. The two circles mark the strongest values.
What we found
Reflectance peaks at 695 nm (r = +0.46): red reflectance rises with disease. It is negative across the NIR (about −0.3 to −0.4) and positive in the SWIR (up to about +0.38).
The derivative reaches r = +0.62 at 800 nm (just beyond the red edge) and −0.56 at 720 nm (on the red-edge peak).
The derivative curve changes sign many times; reflectance changes smoothly.
What it means

The first derivative carries a stronger disease signal than reflectance (0.62 vs 0.46). The opposite signs at 720 and 800 nm describe the same event: the red-edge peak becomes lower and shifts to shorter wavelengths, so the slope falls at 720 nm and rises at 800 nm. This explains why derivative bands dominate the selected features.
Say to the chairman
"The derivative at 800 nm is the single best indicator (r = 0.62); the derivative is consistently stronger than plain reflectance."

blocks.text: 7.3 Effective ranges and optimal wavelengths

blocks.caption: R² of (a) NDSI and (b) RSI with the leaf grade for all band pairs (white contour: effective-range threshold; star: best pair). (report Figure 9)

parts: What it shows
For every combination of two wavelengths, how well the normalised difference (a) or ratio (b) of those two bands predicts the grade.
How to read it

Each point of the map is one band pair (λ_{1} on the horizontal axis, λ_{2} on the vertical). Colour = R² with the grade (dark blue 0, dark red 0.36). The maps are symmetric about the diagonal. The white contour encloses the top 5% of pairs (R² ≥ 0.23); the star marks the best pair.
What we found
No pair reached the planned threshold of R² = 0.5; the best was **(795, 805) nm with R² = 0.36** for both NDSI and RSI.
The highest values form a narrow corner where one band lies in the visible/red edge and the other on the NIR shoulder (around 750–850 nm), and a second area within the SWIR (1400–1900 nm).
The effective ranges defined by the contour were 515–1365, 1380–1395, 1405–1895 and 2020–2105 nm (292 bands at 5-nm spacing).
What it means

Two-band indices capture at most about a third of the variation in leaf grade. The best pair is two very close bands on the NIR shoulder – in effect a measure of the slope there, which links it directly to the derivative at 800 nm. Because no pair reached R² 0.5, the fall-back rule (top 5%) was used, as planned in the methodology.
Say to the chairman
"The best two-band index is NDSI(795, 805) with R² 0.36; the useful band pairs lie at the red edge–NIR shoulder and in the shortwave infrared."

blocks.caption: SHAP-CARS: (a) SHAP importance of all candidate bands, (b) choice of PLS components, (c) one CARS run, (d) selection frequency over 20 runs. (report Figure 10)

parts: What it shows
The four stages of the band selection.
How to read it
(a) Mean |SHAP| of each candidate band (red = derivative, blue = reflectance); the dashed line marks the top-40% cut.
(b) Cross-validated error (RMSE) of PLS against the number of components; the red line marks the number chosen.
(c) One CARS run: black = number of bands still kept, red = cross-validated error; the dotted line marks the iteration with the lowest error.
(d) How often each band was selected in 20 CARS runs; the dashed line marks 50%.
What we found
(a) The largest SHAP values are derivative bands near 680–870 nm and near 1800 nm; reflectance bands contribute little.
(b) The error fell steadily up to 15 components, so 15 were used.
(c) CARS reduced about 110 bands to a few dozen within the first iterations; the error was lowest early (around iteration 5) and rose when too many bands were removed.
(d) Twenty-three bands were selected in at least 70% of runs; the 15 most frequent (FD1090 and FD565 in every run) were kept, all of them derivatives.
What it means

The model-based selection agrees with the correlation curves: the derivative carries the information. Repeating CARS 20 times and keeping only frequently chosen bands protects against the randomness of a single run.
Say to the chairman
"SHAP removed the uninformative bands, CARS chose the best combination, and over 20 runs 15 derivative bands were chosen consistently."

blocks.caption: Optimal wavelengths selected by SHAP-CARS on all leaves. (report Table 22)

parts: What it shows
The 15 optimal wavelengths with their type, spectral region, CARS selection frequency and SHAP importance.
How to read it
"CARS frequency" = share of the 20 runs in which the band was selected; "mean |SHAP|" = its average contribution to the XGBoost predictions.
What we found
All 15 are first-derivative bands: 4 in the visible (FD550, FD565, FD595, FD665), 10 in the NIR (760–1245 nm) and 1 in the SWIR (FD1660).
The bands with the largest SHAP values are FD860 (0.110), FD810 (0.106) and FD1060 (0.089); FD1090 and FD565 were chosen in every run.
What it means

The selected bands cover the green peak and red absorption (pigments), the NIR shoulder and plateau (structure) and one SWIR band (water/dry matter). A high CARS frequency and a high SHAP value are different things: a band can be chosen often because it adds unique information even if its average contribution is small.
Say to the chairman
"Fifteen derivative bands were chosen – mostly on the NIR shoulder, plus green, red and one shortwave-infrared band."

blocks.caption: Optimal wavelengths marked on the mean reflectance (a) and first-derivative (b) spectra. (report Figure 11)

parts: What it shows
Where the 15 selected bands lie on the average spectrum.
How to read it
Red vertical lines mark the selected wavelengths; panel (a) has none because no reflectance band was selected.
What we found
The lines cluster around the green peak (550–595 nm), the red absorption (665 nm), the red-edge shoulder and NIR (760–1090 nm), with single bands at 1245 and 1660 nm.
What it means

The selection is physically sensible: it picks the slopes on both sides of the green peak, the red edge and the NIR plateau, and the flank of the 1450-nm water band. These are the regions a UAV hyperspectral camera must cover.
Say to the chairman
"The chosen bands sit exactly on the parts of the spectrum that respond to chlorophyll, leaf structure and water."

blocks.text: 7.4 Indices and the disease-specific feature set

blocks.caption: White Rust Index (WRI) by grade: (a) distributions, (b) all leaves with mean ± SD. (report Figure 12)

parts: What it shows
The best three-band index found by the search, and how its value changes with grade.
How to read it
(a) Violin and box plots of the index for each grade; (b) every leaf as a dot (slightly spread sideways), with the mean ± SD per grade in black.
What we found
The search returned WRI = NDSI(780, 830) with a third-band weight w = 0, i.e. the third band (400 nm) adds nothing. Correlation with grade r = −0.59.
The mean WRI falls steadily from about +0.003 (grade 0) to about −0.007 (grade 9), but the spread within each grade is large and the distributions overlap.
The next best candidates were almost identical (|r| 0.592–0.595).
What it means

For leaf spectra, a third band did not improve the best two-band contrast: the NIR-shoulder slope already carries the signal. The index orders the grades correctly on average, but a single leaf cannot be graded from it reliably because of the overlap.
Say to the chairman
"A three-band White Rust Index did not beat the two-band NIR-shoulder index; it ranks grades on average, but leaves overlap."

blocks.caption: Correlation among the indices kept after the |r| ≥ 0.95 filter. (report Figure 13)

parts: What it shows
How the 23 remaining indices correlate with each other.
How to read it
Each cell is the correlation between two indices: dark red = +1, dark blue = −1, white = 0.
What we found
The redundancy filter reduced 47 index features (41 published, 3 red-edge parameters, 3 data-driven) to 23.
A large block of greenness and red-edge indices (RSI_best, HI, PSSR, REP, NDVI850, RDVI, PRI, MTVI2) still correlate at 0.7–0.9 with each other.
DWSI-2, MCARI, PSSRc and TCARI are only weakly related to the others.
What it means

Even after removing near-duplicates, many indices measure almost the same thing (greenness and the red edge). The few independent indices (DWSI-2, MCARI) are valuable because they add different information, which is exactly what ReliefF and the VIF check reward.
Say to the chairman
"Most indices tell the same greenness story; only a few, like DWSI-2, add something different."

blocks.caption: ReliefF weights of the indices for detection and six grades, and RReliefF weights for the score (dark blue: top five, selected). (report Figure 14)

parts: What it shows
The ranking of the indices by ReliefF for each task.
How to read it
Longer bar = more useful for separating neighbouring leaves of different classes (or different scores). Dark blue bars are the five selected.
What we found
Detection: RSI_best, HI, REP, RVSI, DWSI-2.
Six grades: REP, RSI_best, HI, DWSI-2, RVSI.
Score: RSI_best, HI, MCARI, PRI, Dr.
What it means

The same core – the best data-driven ratio (RSI_best), the Healthy Index (HI) and the red-edge position (REP) – is chosen for all tasks, supported by the disease–water stress index DWSI-2 and the red-edge stress index RVSI. For the score, pigment indices (MCARI, PRI) and the red-edge height (Dr) enter.
Say to the chairman
"ReliefF picked the same core indices for all three tasks: the NIR-shoulder ratio, the Healthy Index and the red-edge position."

blocks.caption: Variance inflation factors of the disease-specific feature set. (report Figure 15)

parts: What it shows
The 11 features left after the variance-inflation check and their VIF.
How to read it
Red = derivative band, green = vegetation index; the dashed line is the limit of 10.
What we found

Twelve features were removed in turn because they overlapped with others, the largest first: FD855 (VIF 119), PRI (93), FD565 (91), FD810 (75), then FD860, RVSI, FD830, RSI_best, FD1660, HI, FD915, MCARI.
The final 11 all have VIF below 10; the highest are FD595 (9.6), DWSI-2 (7.7) and REP (6.8).
What it means

Several strong features (RSI_best, HI, FD810) were removed not because they are poor, but because their information is already contained in the remaining features. The final set is compact and each feature contributes something of its own.
Say to the chairman
"After removing overlap, 11 features remain – eight derivative bands and three indices – each carrying its own information."

rows: NIR plateau slope beyond the red edge (mesophyll scattering)
slope at the red chlorophyll absorption
slope from the green peak towards the red (pigments)
blocks.caption: Disease-specific feature set (Objective 1, all leaves). (report Table 23)

parts: What it shows
The disease-specific feature set: each feature, whether it is a derivative band or an index, its VIF, its correlation with grade and its physical meaning.
What we found
Eight derivative bands (FD1090, FD1060, FD550, FD1245, FD870, FD760, FD665, FD595) and three indices (DWSI-2, Dr, REP).
Strongest single correlations with grade: REP (−0.50), FD870 (+0.49), Dr (−0.38).
What it means
The set covers pigments (FD550, FD595, FD665, Dr, REP), leaf structure (FD760, FD870, FD1060, FD1090) and water (FD1245, DWSI-2). It is the main input of all models in Objective 2.
Say to the chairman
"This is the disease-specific feature set: 11 features covering chlorophyll, leaf structure and water."

blocks.caption: Distribution of each disease-specific feature by grade. (report Figure 16)

parts: What it shows
Box plots of each of the 11 features for the six grades, with their correlation r.
How to read it
Each box spans the middle 50% of leaves of a grade, the line inside is the median and the whiskers show the range.
What we found
REP falls clearly with grade (medians from about 710 to 700 nm); FD870 rises; Dr falls.
For most features the boxes of neighbouring grades overlap heavily – for example grades 3, 5 and 7 have very similar FD1245, FD760 and DWSI-2.
What it means

Each feature shifts with grade on average, but no single feature separates neighbouring grades. This is why combinations of features are modelled, and why even the best models confuse neighbouring grades (Chapter 8).
Say to the chairman
"Every feature moves with the grade, but neighbouring grades overlap – combining features is necessary."

blocks.caption: Principal component scores of leaf reflectance with 95% ellipses of each grade. (report Figure 17)

parts: What it shows
A two-dimensional summary of the full reflectance spectra: each dot is a leaf placed by its first two principal components.
How to read it
PC1 (55.6% of the variation) and PC2 (32.4%) are the two directions in which the spectra vary most. Large dots are the grade centroids; ellipses contain 95% of the leaves of each grade.
What we found
The grade centroids move in order from upper left (grades 0–1) towards lower right (grade 9).
The ellipses overlap almost completely; the leaves form two clouds, which reflect differences between dates and stages rather than grades.
What it means

The largest sources of variation in the spectra are not the disease: they are leaf and crop differences (stage, date, leaf position). The disease is a smaller, consistent shift within this variation. This is why supervised selection (SHAP-CARS, ReliefF) is needed rather than relying on the main directions of variation.
Say to the chairman
"Disease shifts the spectra in a consistent direction, but this shift is smaller than the natural differences between leaves and dates."

blocks.text: 7.5 Was the selection stable across folds?

blocks.caption: Feature selection repeated inside each outer training part. (report Table 24)

parts: What it shows
The result of repeating the whole Objective 1 selection inside each outer training part.
How to read it
Each row is one fold: the optimal wavelengths found, the best NDSI/RSI pair, the WRI and the disease-specific set of each task.
What we found
The best NDSI and RSI pair was (795, 805) nm in all three folds; the WRI was NDSI(780, 830) or NDSI(785, 835).
The disease-specific sets differ in detail but always contain FD1060, FD1090 and FD760; REP is in the detection and six-grade sets of every fold.
Fold 3 selected two bands near 1800 nm (FD1805, FD1810), at the edge of the 1940-nm water band, that the other folds did not.
What it means

The core of the signal (the NIR-shoulder index, the red-edge position and a few NIR derivative bands) is reproduced in every fold, while the remaining choices vary because many bands carry similar information. This variation is expected and is the reason selection had to be repeated inside each fold for honest testing.
Say to the chairman
"The key features came back in every fold; the details vary because neighbouring bands are interchangeable."

blocks.caption: Number of outer folds in which each optimal wavelength was selected. (report Figure 18)

parts: What it shows
How often each of the 29 distinct optimal wavelengths was chosen across the three folds.
How to read it
Bar height 3 = chosen in all folds, 1 = in one fold only.
What we found
Four bands were chosen in all three folds (FD1060, FD1090, FD1245, FD760); eight in two folds; seventeen in only one.
What it means
The four always-selected bands – two NIR plateau slopes, the red-edge shoulder and the edge of the 1450-nm water band – are the most reliable wavelengths for white rust in these data.
Say to the chairman
"Four wavelengths were chosen every time: 760, 1060, 1090 and 1245 nm derivatives."

blocks.text: 8. Results of Objective 2: how well can white rust be detected and graded?
8.1 What the machine-learning models selected

blocks.caption: Sequential floating forward selection and grid search (inner score: macro-F1 for A and B, negative RMSE for C). (report Table 25)

parts: What it shows
For each task and machine-learning model: how many candidate features were available, how many SFFS kept, the inner cross-validation score and the settings chosen in fold 1.
How to read it
Columns 3–5 are averages over the three folds. The inner score is macro-F1 for tasks A and B and minus RMSE for task C (so −2.01 is better than −2.10).
What we found
From about 11 candidates the models kept 5–9 features; k-NN and PLS kept the fewest.
Inner scores were close between SVM, RF and XGBoost (detection 0.80–0.82, six grades 0.37–0.38, score RMSE 2.01–2.03); PLS-DA/PLSR were clearly lower.
Typical settings: SVM C = 10; RF with 500 trees and minimum leaf size 1–3; XGBoost with shallow trees (depth 3–5) and a low learning rate (0.05).
What it means

Compact models with 6–9 features are enough; adding more features did not improve the inner score by more than 1%. The inner scores already predict the final ranking: the non-linear models (SVM, RF, XGBoost) beat the linear PLS models, meaning that the relationship between spectra and grade is not purely linear.
Say to the chairman
"Each model needed only 6–9 features; the non-linear models were clearly better than the linear PLS models."

blocks.text: 8.2 How the networks trained

blocks.caption: Deep-learning runs (validation score: macro-F1 on the validation plots, tasks A and B). (report Table 26)

parts: What it shows
The size of each network, how long it trained before early stopping, and its best validation score.
How to read it

"Parameters" = number of trainable weights; "Epochs" = median number of passes over the training data before early stopping (9 runs = 3 folds × tasks); validation score = macro-F1 on the validation plots.
What we found
The networks range from 3 thousand weights (DNN-F1) to 11 million (ResNet18). DT-EDNet has 0.95 million.
The image networks stopped after a median of 31–42 epochs; DNN-F1 trained longer (81).
Best validation scores were all between 0.616 and 0.638 – essentially the same.
What it means

Having 1000–4000 times more weights than DNN-F1 did not give the image networks a better validation score. With 1500 training leaves and 10–16 features there is far less information than these networks were designed for, so they reach their limit quickly.
Say to the chairman
"Networks with millions of weights reached the same validation score as a tiny dense network."

blocks.caption: Training and validation loss and validation macro-F1 of the four pseudo-image networks (fold 1, six grades). (report Figure 19)

parts: What it shows
How the four image networks learned during training in fold 1 for the six-grade task.
How to read it

Blue = training loss (error on the training leaves), orange = validation loss (error on held-out validation plots), green = validation macro-F1 (right axis). The dotted line marks the best epoch kept by early stopping.
What we found
Training loss falls steadily in all four networks.
Validation loss stops improving after a few epochs and then rises (most clearly for DT-EDNet and ResNet18).
Validation macro-F1 stays flat at about 0.30–0.40; the best epochs were 10 (DT-EDNet), 13 (EfficientNet-B0), 5 (ResNet18) and 28 (ConvNeXt V2-Atto).
What it means

This is the classic picture of **over-fitting**: after the first few epochs the networks start memorising the training leaves instead of learning patterns that hold for new plots. Early stopping on the validation plots kept the best epoch, so the test results are not affected by the over-fitting, but it shows that the networks are too large for this amount of leaf data.
Say to the chairman
"The networks learn the useful pattern within a few epochs and then start memorising; early stopping protects the results."

blocks.text: 8.3 Test results of all models
The three tables below are the core results of Objective 2. All numbers are pooled test predictions: every one of the 2330 leaves was predicted once, by a model trained without its replication.

blocks.caption: Task A – detection: test metrics (pooled over the three outer folds; n = 2330 leaves). (report Table 27)

parts: What it shows
Detection (healthy vs diseased) results of the 10 models, best first.
How to read it
Macro-F1 is the main metric; "± SD folds" is its spread over the three test folds. Sensitivity = share of diseased leaves found; specificity = share of healthy leaves correctly called healthy.
What we found
Best: SVM (macro-F1 0.792 ± 0.007, AUC 0.897) and DNN-F1 (0.790 ± 0.009, AUC 0.896), followed by ResNet18 (0.785) and ConvNeXt V2-Atto (0.783).

SVM is balanced: sensitivity 0.831 and specificity 0.833. EfficientNet-B0, RF, k-NN and PLS-DA find more diseased leaves (sensitivity 0.85–0.92) but at the cost of calling many healthy leaves diseased (specificity 0.48–0.71).
DT-EDNet: macro-F1 0.759, AUC 0.852 – eighth of ten.
What it means

A diseased leaf can be recognised from its spectrum with about 83% accuracy in both directions, under a strict test on unseen replications. The top four models are within about one fold-to-fold SD of each other, so they should be regarded as equally good; SVM is preferred because it is simple and balanced.
Say to the chairman
"Detection is reliable: the SVM finds 83% of diseased leaves and correctly clears 83% of healthy ones, AUC 0.90."

blocks.caption: Task B – six grades: test metrics and F1 of each grade. (report Table 28)

parts: What it shows
Six-grade results of the 10 models, with the F1 of each grade.
How to read it
Overall accuracy (OA) and macro-F1 count only exact hits; QWK and "±1 grade" give credit for near-misses. The F1 columns show how well each grade is recognised.
What we found
Best macro-F1: ConvNeXt V2-Atto 0.360 (QWK 0.633, 75.5% within one grade), then RF 0.349, SVM 0.346, DNN-F1 0.344, XGBoost 0.342.
Exact accuracy is only 0.35–0.40 for all models, but 70–76% of leaves are within one grade and QWK is 0.59–0.63 for the good models.
Grade 0 is recognised best (F1 0.59–0.70), grade 1 next (about 0.40); grades 3, 5 and 9 are the weakest (F1 often 0.15–0.35).
PLS-DA failed on the extreme grades (F1 0.00 for grade 9).
What it means

Exact six-grade classification of single leaves is not achievable with leaf spectra alone: about two leaves in five are placed in the exact grade. But the errors are mostly small – three leaves in four land in the right grade or the next one – and QWK above 0.6 means substantial agreement on the ordered scale. The models capture the severity **order**, not the exact visual category.
Say to the chairman
"Exact grades are right for only 39% of leaves, but 75% are within one grade – the models get the order right, not the exact class."

blocks.caption: Task C – severity score: test metrics (grade units). (report Table 29)

parts: What it shows
Severity-score (0–9) results of the 10 models.
How to read it
R² = share of the variation in grade explained; RMSE and MAE in grade units; RPD = SD of observed grades / RMSE; bias = mean of predicted − observed; r = correlation.
What we found
Best: XGBoost R² 0.459, RMSE 2.04, MAE 1.58, RPD 1.36, r 0.68; RF (0.449), DNN-F1 (0.448) and SVR (0.445) are very close.
All models have a small negative bias (−0.01 to −0.32): they slightly under-predict on average.
RPD is 1.27–1.36 for all models, below the 1.4 often used as the limit of "fair".
What it means

The score is predicted with moderate accuracy: the typical error is about 1.6–2.0 grade units, i.e. about one step on the 0, 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 scale. The score is useful for ranking leaves and for following severity over time, but it is not precise enough to replace visual grading of individual leaves.
Say to the chairman
"The severity score explains 46% of the variation with a typical error of about 2 grade units – useful for ranking, not for exact grading."

blocks.caption: Model comparison: macro-F1 for detection and six grades (± SD over folds) and R² for the severity score (blue: machine learning; purple: deep learning). (report Figure 20)

parts: What it shows
The main metric of every model for the three tasks, side by side.
How to read it
Bars are sorted from best to worst; blue = machine learning, purple = deep learning; the small whiskers show the SD over the three folds.
What we found
Detection: SVM 0.792 and DNN-F1 0.790 lead; nine of ten models are between 0.72 and 0.79.
Six grades: ConvNeXt V2-Atto 0.360 leads, but the next six models (RF, SVM, DNN-F1, XGBoost, ResNet18, DT-EDNet) are within 0.023 of it.
Score: XGBoost 0.459 leads; RF, DNN-F1 and SVR follow within 0.015.
What it means

Machine-learning and deep-learning models are interleaved in every ranking; neither family is consistently better. The whiskers of the leading models overlap, so the differences between them are within the normal variation between replications.
Say to the chairman
"Machine learning and deep learning are mixed in every ranking – the differences between the best models are within the noise."

blocks.caption: All metrics of all models (darker = better within each column). (report Figure 21)

parts: What it shows
Every metric of every model as a colour table, separately for the three tasks.
How to read it
Each column is one metric; darker green = better within that column (for RMSE and MAE lower is better). Read across a row to see a model's profile.
What we found
Detection: SVM and DNN-F1 are dark in almost every column; PLS-DA has the highest sensitivity (0.92) but the lowest specificity (0.48).
Six grades: ConvNeXt V2-Atto is darkest for macro-F1, QWK and within-one; SVM has the highest exact accuracy (0.40).
Score: XGBoost is darkest for R², RMSE, RPD and r; SVR has the lowest MAE (1.56).
What it means

Different metrics can favour different models, which is why several metrics are reported. A model that maximises sensitivity (PLS-DA) is not the best overall; balanced models are preferred for disease surveillance, where false alarms also have a cost.
Say to the chairman
"The heat map shows that the top models are good across all metrics, not just the main one."

blocks.caption: Confusion matrices (counts and row percentages) of the best machine-learning (RF) and deep-learning (ConvNeXt V2-Atto) models for six grades. (report Figure 22)

parts: What it shows
Where the six-grade predictions go: for each observed grade (rows), how many leaves were predicted in each grade (columns).
How to read it
Each cell shows the number of leaves and the percentage of its row; darker green = higher share; the outlined diagonal cells are correct predictions. Cells next to the diagonal are one-grade errors.
What we found
Grade 0: 70% (RF) and 67% (ConvNeXt) correct; most errors go to grade 1.
Grade 1: 38% and 43% correct; errors spread mainly to grades 0 and 3.
Grade 3: only 13% (RF) and 28% (ConvNeXt) correct; many grade-3 leaves were predicted as grade 5 (27% in RF).
Grade 5: 34% (RF) correct but only 19% for ConvNeXt, which put 30% of grade-5 leaves in grade 3 and 24% in grade 7.
Grade 9: 29% and 33% correct; 26–28% were predicted as grade 7 and 30% (RF) as grade 5.
What it means

The errors pile up next to the diagonal: the models confuse neighbouring grades far more than distant ones. This is exactly the pattern expected when neighbouring grades overlap spectrally and when the visual scale itself is uncertain between adjacent grades (Bock et al., 2010). Gross errors (for example grade 9 predicted as 0) are rare (2%).
Say to the chairman
"Most mistakes are one grade off; a severe leaf is almost never called healthy."

blocks.caption: ROC curves for detection (solid: machine learning; dashed: deep learning). (report Figure 23)

parts: What it shows
The trade-off between finding diseased leaves and raising false alarms, for every detection model.
How to read it

Each curve traces sensitivity (vertical) against the false-positive rate (horizontal) as the decision threshold changes. A curve close to the upper-left corner is better; the diagonal dotted line is chance. The area under the curve (AUC) is given in the legend.
What we found
SVM (AUC 0.897) and DNN-F1 (0.896) have the highest curves; RF, ResNet18, XGBoost, ConvNeXt, EfficientNet and DT-EDNet follow (0.85–0.88); k-NN and PLS-DA are lowest (0.84).
At a false-positive rate of 10%, SVM and DNN-F1 still find about 75% of diseased leaves; at 20% they find about 86%.
What it means

All models are far above chance. The ROC curve shows that the decision threshold can be moved depending on the purpose: an early-warning system can accept more false alarms to catch more diseased leaves, while a fungicide decision might demand fewer false alarms.
Say to the chairman
"All models are well above chance; the best reach AUC 0.90, and the threshold can be tuned to the purpose."

blocks.caption: Six-grade performance profile (F1 of each grade, OA, kappa and macro-F1). (report Figure 24)

parts: What it shows
A "spider" chart comparing the five networks and the best tree model (XGBoost) on the F1 of each grade and three summary metrics.
How to read it
Each axis is one metric (0 at the centre, higher further out). A larger polygon is better; the shape shows which grades a model handles well.
What we found
All polygons extend furthest towards "F1 grade 0" (0.59–0.67) and are small towards grades 3, 5 and 9.
DT-EDNet has the best F1 for grade 5 (0.39); DNN-F1 is relatively strong for grade 9 (0.28); ConvNeXt is strongest for grades 0 and 3.
What it means

The models share the same strengths and weaknesses: healthy leaves are recognised, the middle grades are not. Differences between models are local (one grade here or there) rather than a general advantage.
Say to the chairman
"All models recognise healthy leaves well and struggle with the middle grades."

blocks.caption: Predicted vs observed severity score of the best machine-learning (XGBoost) and deep-learning (DNN-F1) models (black: mean ± SD per grade). (report Figure 25)

parts: What it shows
For every leaf, the predicted severity score against its visual grade.
How to read it
Each coloured dot is a leaf (spread sideways within its grade); black squares are the mean prediction per grade with ± SD bars; the dashed line is the 1:1 line of perfect prediction.
What we found
XGBoost mean predictions: grade 0 → 1.2, 1 → 2.3, 3 → 3.5, 5 → 4.1, 7 → 4.9, 9 → 5.3. DNN-F1 is similar (1.1 to 5.0).
The SD within each grade is about 1.1–1.6 grade units.
What it means

The predictions increase with the true grade, so the ranking is right, but the line is flatter than 1:1: low grades are over-predicted and high grades are under-predicted. This "shrinkage towards the mean" is typical when the inputs explain only part of the variation; the model hedges towards the middle of the scale. It means the score should be calibrated before being used as an absolute severity value, especially for severe leaves.
Say to the chairman
"Predictions follow the grade but are pulled towards the middle: a grade-9 leaf is predicted at about 5."

blocks.text: 8.4 Feature configurations and the DT-EDNet ablation

blocks.caption: Macro-F1 (six grades) of the networks on the three feature configurations. (report Table 30)

parts: What it shows
Six-grade macro-F1 of the four image networks when fed with three different feature sets.
How to read it
OW = the 15 optimal wavelengths; VI = the five selected indices; DSF = the disease-specific feature set (11 features).
What we found
ConvNeXt V2-Atto was best overall with OW (0.371).
DT-EDNet did best with DSF (0.337), followed by VI (0.334) and OW (0.319).
Differences between configurations are 0.02–0.04 for each network.
What it means

No feature set is best for every network, and the differences are about the size of the fold-to-fold variation. The compact DSF is a sound default; the 15 optimal wavelengths can help a network that can exploit many inputs.
Caution
The original report text stated that DT-EDNet did best on the optimal wavelengths; the table shows it did best on the DSF (0.337 vs 0.319 for OW).
Say to the chairman
"The choice of feature set changes the networks by only 0.02–0.04 macro-F1."

blocks.caption: Networks on the three feature configurations (six grades). (report Figure 26)

parts: What it shows
The same comparison as the table, as grouped bars.
How to read it
Light blue = OW, green = VI, purple = DSF, for each network.
What we found
All bars lie between 0.32 and 0.37 macro-F1.
What it means
The networks are limited by the information in the leaf spectra, not by the particular way the features are chosen.
Say to the chairman
"Whatever features they get, the networks land between 0.32 and 0.37."

blocks.caption: DT-EDNet module ablation (six grades; SE = squeeze-and-excitation, DTG = dual transformer group). (report Table 31)

parts: What it shows
What happens to DT-EDNet when its special modules are removed.
How to read it
DT-EDNet-DTG = without the dual transformer group; DT-EDNet-SE = without the squeeze-and-excitation block; DT-EDNet-SE-DTG = without both. Macro-recall = average recall over grades.
What we found
Full DT-EDNet: macro-F1 0.337, QWK 0.592.
Without SE: 0.319 (−0.018); without DTG: 0.326 (−0.011); without both: 0.327 (−0.010).
QWK fell more clearly without DTG (0.533) or without both (0.543) than without SE (0.579).
What it means

Each module adds a little, but the changes (0.01–0.02 macro-F1) are smaller than the fold-to-fold variation and not additive (removing both is not worse than removing one). On 4 × 4 pseudo-images there is little spatial structure for attention modules to use, so their benefit cannot show; the paper designed them for real hyperspectral images of canopies.
Caution

The original report discussion said the dual transformer group mattered more; the table shows removing SE lowered macro-F1 more (0.319) than removing DTG (0.326). Both effects are small. In the figure title DTG is written as "dual-token gating"; it is the dual transformer group of DT-EDNet.
Say to the chairman
"Removing DT-EDNet's modules changes it by only 0.01–0.02 – at leaf level its special design has little to work with."

blocks.caption: DT-EDNet module ablation (six grades). (report Figure 27)

parts: What it shows
The ablation as grouped bars for four metrics.
How to read it
For each variant: OA, kappa, macro-recall and macro-F1.
What we found
The full network has the highest OA (0.39) and kappa (0.24); the variants are 0.35–0.37 and 0.21–0.22. Macro-recall is about the same (0.33–0.35) for all.
What it means
The full DT-EDNet is slightly more accurate overall, but its ability to recognise the individual grades (macro-recall) is not improved by the modules at leaf level.
Say to the chairman
"The full DT-EDNet is marginally better, but within the noise."

blocks.text: 8.5 Which features drive the predictions? (SHAP)

blocks.caption: SHAP summary for the severity score and SHAP importance by grade for six grades (XGBoost on the disease-specific feature set). (report Figure 28)

parts: What it shows
(a) How each feature pushes the predicted severity score up or down; (b) how important each feature is for recognising each grade.
How to read it

(a) Each dot is a leaf. Its horizontal position is the SHAP value: right of zero = the feature raised the predicted score for that leaf, left = lowered it. Colour = the feature value (red = high, blue = low). Features are ordered by importance.
(b) Mean |SHAP| for each feature, split by grade (colours); longer bars = more important.
What we found
Most important for the score: FD870 (mean |SHAP| 0.89), REP (0.58), FD1060 (0.50), FD1245 (0.37), FD665 (0.34), then DWSI-2, FD595, FD1090, Dr, FD760 and FD550.
Directions: high FD870, high FD1245, high DWSI-2 and high FD595 raise the score; high REP, high FD1060, high FD665 and high Dr lower it.
For six grades, FD870 is again the most important, contributing most to recognising grade 0 and grade 9; FD550 is important mainly for grade 1.
What it means

The model uses the features in physically sensible ways. A low red-edge position (shifted towards the blue) and a low red-edge peak (Dr) mean less chlorophyll and a higher score; a steeper slope at 870 nm reflects the shifted red edge; a higher DWSI-2 (R_{1660}/R_{550}) and a higher slope at 1245 nm reflect drier tissue. The model is therefore not relying on an artefact: it reads chlorophyll, structure and water.
Say to the chairman
"The models rely on the red-edge position and the near-infrared slope, in the direction expected from chlorophyll loss – they read real physiology."

blocks.text: 8.6 Is the performance consistent across groups?

blocks.caption: Six-grade macro-F1 by growth stage, variety, leaf position and sampling date (RF and ConvNeXt V2-Atto). (report Figure 29)

parts: What it shows
The six-grade macro-F1 of the best machine-learning (RF, blue) and deep-learning (ConvNeXt, purple) model computed separately within each group.
How to read it
Each pair of bars is one group; n = number of leaves.
What we found
Growth stage: 0.28–0.33 (vegetative lowest). Variety: 0.33–0.38. Leaf position: 0.32–0.38 (LL highest).
Date: 0.22 on 11 February, 0.28–0.32 on the later dates.
Detection was similarly stable (SVM macro-F1 0.76–0.80 by stage, variety and leaf position) except on 11 February (0.67), and the score R² was 0.38–0.48 by variety, leaf position and timing.
What it means

Performance does not depend strongly on variety or leaf position. It is lower on 11 February because almost all leaves were grade 0–1 on that date: with little range of disease, the grades are harder to tell apart and R² within that date is even negative for the score (RMSE 1.35, small, but the variance within the date is also small). The models work best when the full range of disease is present.
Say to the chairman
"Results are similar across varieties, stages and leaf positions; only the first date, with very little disease, is weaker."

blocks.caption: Leave-one-variety-out and leave-one-timing-out tests (random forest). (report Figure 30)

parts: What it shows
What happens when a model is applied to a variety (or sowing date) that it never saw during training.
How to read it
(a) Six-grade macro-F1 on the held-out group; (b) severity-score RMSE on the held-out group. Dark bars = varieties, light bars = sowing timings.
What we found
Six grades: held-out varieties V1 0.37, V2 0.39, V3 0.34; held-out timings D1 0.37, D2 0.31, D3 0.34, D4 0.40.
Score RMSE 1.91–2.23 (R² 0.37–0.53), close to the cross-validated 2.04–2.06.
What it means

A model trained on two varieties works as well on the third, and a model trained on three sowing dates works on the fourth. The spectral signal of white rust is therefore not specific to one variety or crop age – an important condition for applying the models to other fields and seasons.
Say to the chairman
"The models work on a variety or sowing date they have never seen – the signal is general."

blocks.text: 8.7 The covariate baseline: do the spectra add information beyond the calendar?

blocks.caption: Covariate-only, spectra and spectra + covariate models on unsprayed leaves (pooled leave-one-replication-out test predictions; B1 = logistic / ordinal logistic / linear model; B2 = SVM, XGBoost, random forest for tasks A, B, C). (report Table 32)

parts: What it shows
The performance of three model types on three kinds of input – covariates only, leaf spectra only, and both – for the 1952 unsprayed leaves.
How to read it
Rows are grouped by input; within each, B1 = interpretable statistical model, random forest, and the best machine-learning model of the task (B2). Higher is better except RMSE.
What we found
**Covariates only** (no spectra): detection macro-F1 0.76–0.78 and AUC 0.93–0.94; six grades 0.29–0.31; score R² 0.32–0.33.
**Leaf spectra only:** detection 0.70–0.73 (lower than covariates); six grades up to 0.36; score R² up to 0.41.
**Spectra + covariates:** the best of all for every task – detection macro-F1 0.82 and AUC 0.96 (RF), six grades 0.41, score R² 0.45.
What it means

The calendar (crop age, sowing date, stage, variety) predicts a large part of the disease level on its own. For the **severity** tasks the spectra do better than the calendar, and the combination is best. For **detection within unsprayed plots** the calendar is better than the spectra – explained below.
Say to the chairman
"Knowing only crop age, sowing date and stage already predicts much of the disease; the spectra beat this baseline for severity, and the combination is best."

blocks.caption: Primary metric of the three models on covariates only, leaf spectra and spectra + covariates (unsprayed, naturally infected leaves; M0 = the stronger covariate-only model). (report Figure 31)

parts: What it shows
The same results as bars: for each task, the main metric of the three models on each input.
How to read it
Grey = interpretable model (logistic, ordinal logistic, linear), green = random forest, purple = best ML model; M0 marks the covariate model used as the baseline.
What we found
Detection: covariates 0.76–0.78 > spectra 0.70–0.73 < spectra + covariates 0.76–0.82.
Six grades: covariates 0.29–0.31 < spectra 0.27–0.36 < spectra + covariates 0.36–0.41.
Score: covariates R² 0.32–0.33 < spectra 0.37–0.41 < spectra + covariates 0.39–0.45.
What it means

The bars rise from left to right for the two severity tasks: each source of information adds to the other. For detection, the dip in the middle shows that within the unsprayed plots the date tells more about healthy vs diseased than the leaf spectrum does.
Say to the chairman
"For severity, spectra beat the calendar and the combination is best; for detection inside infected plots, the date says more."

blocks.caption: Gains with 95% plot-block bootstrap confidence intervals (2000 resamples). ✓ = real gain: interval excludes zero, larger than the fold-to-fold SD and the same sign in all three folds; ✗ = a real loss by the same rule. For RMSE a negative value is an improvement. (report Table 33)

parts: What it shows
The three gains with their 95% bootstrap intervals, and whether each gain meets the strict "real gain" rule.
How to read it

ΔS = what the spectra add over the covariate baseline; ΔC = what the covariates add to the spectra; ΔT = both together over the baseline. ✓ = real gain, ✗ = real loss; unmarked = not consistent enough to be called real. For RMSE a negative value is an improvement.
What we found
**Detection:** ΔS −0.078 macro-F1 and −0.199 balanced accuracy (a real loss ✗); ΔC +0.099; ΔT +0.021 (−0.031 to +0.070), not a real gain.
What it means

Under a strict test, the leaf spectra add real information about **severity** that the calendar cannot provide: leaves of the same date, sowing and stage differ in their actual infection, and the spectra see that difference. For **detection inside the unsprayed plots** the spectra lose to the calendar – see the explanation box below.
Say to the chairman
"The spectra give a real, statistically confirmed gain for grades (+0.043) and score (+0.083 R²) beyond what the calendar predicts."

blocks.label: Why the calendar beats the spectra for detection inside unsprayed plots.
text: On 11 February 46% of the unsprayed leaves were still grade 0; on the later dates only 0–3% were. So within the unsprayed plots "healthy" almost means "first date", and the date alone separates most healthy from diseased leaves.

This does not make the spectra useless for detection. A sensor surveying an unknown field does not know the sampling calendar of this experiment; and when the sprayed healthy plots are included (Chapter 8.3), the spectra detect disease with macro-F1 0.79 and AUC 0.90. The baseline shows that, in this experiment, time is a strong predictor that any honest evaluation has to account for.

blocks.caption: Gains of the spectra (ΔS), of the covariates added to the spectra (ΔC) and of both (ΔT) with 95% plot-block bootstrap intervals (filled = real difference). (report Figure 32)

parts: What it shows
The gains of the previous table as points with interval bars.
How to read it

Blue = ΔS, orange = ΔC, purple = ΔT. The vertical line is zero; right of zero = better (except RMSE, where left = better). Filled circles meet all three conditions of a real difference; open circles do not.
What we found
Six grades: all three macro-F1 gains are filled and right of zero.
Score: ΔS and ΔT are filled for both R² and RMSE.

How to read it

Each point is the effect of a one-SD change in the covariate (or of a level compared with its reference, e.g. D4 vs D1), with its 95% interval. Red = raises disease, blue = lowers it, grey = not significant. Units: log-odds (detection, grades) or grade units (score).
What we found

**Crop age (DAS)** has by far the largest effect: +5.0 log-odds per SD for detection, +2.77 for grades and +2.77 grade units for the score; its square is negative for grades (−0.38) and score (−0.21), i.e. the rise slows down.
**Later sowing raises disease at the same crop age:** D2, D3, D4 vs D1 = +0.89, +1.74, +3.05 log-odds (detection), +0.49, +0.83, +1.73 (grades) and +0.54, +0.87, +1.72 grade units (score).
**Growth stage** has a negative effect once crop age is accounted for (−0.66 grades, −0.60 score).
**Variety V3** has less disease than V1 (−0.28 grades, −0.33 score); V2 slightly less (−0.11, −0.12).
What it means

Disease increases strongly with crop age, as expected for a natural epidemic. At the same crop age, a later-sown crop is observed later in the season – for example D4 at 63 days on 13 March against D1 at 64 days on 11 February – when the epidemic and its inoculum had built up much further; the timing effect therefore largely carries calendar time. Variety V3 is somewhat more tolerant. These effects are why a model without spectra already predicts so much – and why the spectra must be judged by what they add beyond them.
Say to the chairman
"Crop age dominates; at the same age, later sowings had more disease, and V3 had the least."

blocks.text: 9. Discussion: what the results mean
9.1 The physical basis of the white rust signal

The spectral changes agree with the biology of white rust. The pathogen destroys chlorophyll around the pustules, which raises red reflectance, lowers the red-edge peak and shifts the red-edge position towards shorter wavelengths (Horler et al., 1983; Filella and Peñuelas, 1994). The 7.7-nm blue shift between grades 0 and 9 is of the size reported for chlorophyll loss in diseased leaves (Mahlein et al., 2013; Meng et al., 2020). The white pustules and the collapse of mesophyll cells change internal scattering, which lowers the near-infrared plateau, and tissue dehydration raises reflectance in the shortwave-infrared water bands (Mishra et al., 2009; Peñuelas et al., 1997).

Two observations add nuance. First, the near-infrared change was not in the same direction at every growth stage (Chapter 7.2), so NIR reflectance alone is not a robust indicator: leaf ageing and pod formation change it as well. Second, the water-band edges (FD1245, and FD1805/FD1810 in one fold) and DWSI-2 entered the selected features, which justifies keeping the water bands in contact-probe data.

blocks.label: One sentence for the chairman.
blocks.text: "White rust removes chlorophyll, damages the leaf structure and dries the tissue; the spectra show all three, and the red-edge position is the clearest single indicator."
9.2 Why derivatives work best

All 15 optimal wavelengths were first-derivative bands, and the derivative correlated more strongly with the grade than reflectance (0.62 vs 0.46). The derivative removes additive differences between leaves – thickness, surface wax, small differences in probe contact – and highlights the shape of the spectrum, especially the red edge (Tsai and Philpot, 1998). This agrees with the DT-EDNet study, where the optimal wavelengths were concentrated in the red edge and near infrared (Ma et al., 2026), and with wheat and rice disease studies that used derivative or red-edge features (Huang et al., 2020; Mandal et al., 2023). The best two-band index, NDSI(795, 805), is in effect a slope on the NIR shoulder, and the White Rust Index search did not find a useful third band: for leaf spectra, a narrow red-edge-to-NIR contrast carries most of the signal.
9.3 Why detection is good but six grades are difficult
Detection reached macro-F1 0.79, but six-grade macro-F1 stayed near 0.36. This gap is common in leaf-level severity work and has three causes:

items: **The grades are steps on a continuum.** A grade-3 leaf and a grade-5 leaf differ only in the area covered by pustules; their spectra differ by small amounts (Chapter 7.4).
**The labels themselves are uncertain.** Visual raters disagree most for intermediate grades (Bock et al., 2010); some of the "errors" of the models are disagreements with an imperfect label.
**The spectral distributions overlap.** The box plots and the PCA show that neighbouring grades overlap for every feature, so no model can separate them sharply.

blocks.text: The ordinal metrics confirm that the errors were small in grade terms (QWK 0.63; 75% within one grade). Similar patterns were reported for wheat yellow rust and Fusarium head blight, where severity classes in the middle of the scale had the lowest accuracy (Huang et al., 2020; Lv et al., 2023), and for rice blast in India (Mandal et al., 2023). The usual remedies – merging grades into three or four classes, or treating severity as a continuous score – are both part of the thesis methodology (four severity classes plus disease-index regression).
9.4 Machine learning versus deep learning

All models performed within a narrow range. For detection, the best network (DNN-F1, 0.790) and the best machine-learning model (SVM, 0.792) differed by 0.002 – less than the fold-to-fold SD (about 0.01). For six grades, ConvNeXt V2-Atto (0.360) and RF (0.349) were within one SD; for the score, XGBoost (R² 0.459) stayed ahead of the best network (DNN-F1, 0.448). DT-EDNet reached 0.759 (detection), 0.337 (six grades) and R² 0.419 (score) and did not exceed the comparison networks at leaf level.

The reason is the input. With 10–16 selected features, the 4 × 4 pseudo-images are an arrangement of numbers rather than a picture (Sharma et al., 2019): neighbouring cells are not neighbouring places on a leaf, so the convolution and attention modules that make these networks powerful on real images have little to use. The ablation agrees – removing DT-EDNet's modules changed macro-F1 by only 0.01–0.02 – and the learning curves show early over-fitting. Tree ensembles and support vector machines are known to be strong on small tabular data. The real test of DT-EDNet will come in the UAV phase, where it receives genuine spatial and spectral patterns, as in the original rice-blast study.

blocks.label: What to say if asked "So is deep learning useless?"
blocks.text: "No. At leaf level the input is a short list of numbers, which is where classical machine learning is strongest. DT-EDNet was designed for hyperspectral images; it will be tested on the UAV images of 2026-27, where it has spatial patterns to learn from."
9.5 The role of the calendar and the weather

Growth stage, sowing date, crop age and sampling date follow the epidemic, so a model without any sensor data already explained much of the disease level (detection macro-F1 0.78 and AUC 0.93 within unsprayed plots; six-grade macro-F1 0.31; score R² 0.33), as expected from weather- and calendar-based disease models (De Wolf and Isard, 2007; Bijlwan et al., 2025).

For severity the spectra added information that the calendar cannot give: six-grade macro-F1 rose by 0.043 and score R² by 0.083 (both real gains), because leaves of the same date, sowing and stage differ in their actual infection. Spectra and covariates together gave the best results (ΔT +0.080 for grades, +0.124 R² for the score), in line with the benefit of combining sensor and weather data reported for wheat diseases (Zhang et al., 2014; Ruan et al., 2022).

Infection was natural, so the weather before sampling matters more than the weather during it. The 17 favourable leaf-infection days occurred between 18 December 2025 and 4 February 2026; none fell in the sampling period. The crops sown on 9 and 18 December were exposed to all 17, the crop sown on 9 January to 7. With four sampling dates the 7-day weather is the same for every leaf of a date, so it describes the epidemic but cannot be tested as an independent predictor; the 13 UAV flights of 2026-27 and the Bharatpur data will allow that.
9.6 Limitations

items: **One season, one location.** External validation (Bharatpur, next season) is needed before the models can be used elsewhere.
**Subjective labels.** Visual leaf grades contain rater error; image-based pustule area or a second rater would reduce label noise (Bock et al., 2010).
**Class imbalance.** Grade 9 had only 132 leaves; class weights reduce but do not remove its disadvantage.
**Confounding of stage and date.** Vegetative leaves occur only on the first two dates and pod-formation leaves only on the last two, so stage and date effects cannot be separated.
**Few healthy leaves in infected plots after the first date.** This is why detection within unsprayed plots depends so much on the date.
**Networks not tuned.** The networks used the paper settings on CPU; tuning could change their ranking slightly.
**No pre-symptomatic data.** Objective 3 could not be addressed; it needs the pre-symptomatic flights of 2026-27.

blocks.text: 9.7 Implications for the UAV phase (2026-27)

items: **Wavelengths:** the red edge (690–760 nm), the NIR shoulder (780–870 nm) and the SWIR water-band edges carry the disease signal; the hyperspectral camera must cover them.
**Features:** keep first-derivative features and the red-edge position; do not rely on NIR reflectance alone.
**Outputs:** detection is realistic at canopy level; severity should be reported as a score or a small number of classes rather than six grades.
**Evaluation:** keep the leave-one-replication-out design and the covariate baseline, so that the sensor is credited only with what it adds beyond the calendar.
**Models:** the saved leaf models can be used to check the UAV predictions on the leaves sampled during the flights; DT-EDNet should be tested on real image patches.

blocks.text: 9.8 Recommendations for data collection in 2026-27
The leaf analysis also shows how the next season's measurements can be made more informative. The following points follow directly from the results:

items: **Sample before symptoms appear.** On the first date 45% of leaves already showed symptoms; Objective 3 needs measurements on dates before visible disease. The three pre-symptomatic UAV flights should be matched by leaf spectra on the same days.

**Keep healthy leaves in the infected plots on every date.** After 11 February almost no unsprayed leaf was grade 0, which made detection within the unsprayed plots depend on the date. Marking a few protected leaves or sub-plots inside each replication would give healthy references on every date.

**Reduce label noise.** A second rater on a subset of leaves, or a photograph of each measured leaf for image-based pustule area, would show how much of the six-grade confusion comes from the visual scale itself (Bock et al., 2010).
**Increase the severe grades.** Grade 9 had only 132 leaves; targeted sampling of severely diseased leaves on the later dates would give the models more examples of the rarest class.
**Spread growth stages across dates.** Where possible, sample leaves of different stages on the same date, so that stage and date effects can be separated.
**Record leaf-level covariates.** Leaf age or node number and the time of measurement help to explain variation that is not disease.

**Keep the evaluation design.** Use leave-one-replication-out validation, nested selection and the covariate baseline for the UAV data as well, so that results remain comparable with this leaf analysis.

blocks.label: Why these recommendations matter.
blocks.text: Each point addresses a limitation identified in this analysis. Together they will make the 2026-27 results stronger and allow Objective 3 and the role of weather to be tested properly.
10. Conclusions

items: White rust lowers near-infrared reflectance, raises red and shortwave-infrared reflectance and shifts the red-edge position by 7.7 nm towards shorter wavelengths between grade 0 and grade 9.

The first derivative carries the strongest signal. SHAP-CARS selected 15 derivative bands; the best two-band index is NDSI(795, 805) (R² 0.36); the disease-specific feature set has 11 features (FD1090, FD1060, FD550, FD1245, FD870, FD760, FD665, FD595, DWSI-2, Dr, REP), with FD760, FD1060, FD1090 and FD1245 selected in every fold.
Detection of diseased leaves is reliable (SVM macro-F1 0.792, AUC 0.897, sensitivity and specificity 0.83).
Six-grade classification is limited by the overlap of neighbouring grades (best macro-F1 0.360) but captures the order of severity (QWK 0.633; 75% within one grade).
The severity score is predicted with R² 0.459 and RMSE 2.04 grades (XGBoost); predictions are compressed towards the middle of the scale.
Machine-learning and deep-learning models performed alike; DT-EDNet did not gain from its attention modules on leaf-level pseudo-images.

A covariate-only model explained much of the epidemic; the spectra added a real gain for six grades (+0.043 macro-F1) and score (+0.083 R²) beyond it, and the models transferred across varieties and sowing dates.
Final models trained on all 2330 leaves are saved, with a prediction script, for the UAV phase and the Bharatpur validation.

blocks.label: The take-home message.
blocks.text: Leaf spectra detect white rust reliably and rank its severity; they show where in the spectrum to look from the UAV; and the evaluation design makes sure the sensor is credited only for what it truly adds.
