blocks.text: Appendix D. Questions the chairman may ask – with answers

blocks.q: Why did you work at leaf level and not with plot means?
blocks.a: The grade is scored on each leaf, so leaf spectra and leaf grades match one to one. Plot means would mix grades and reduce 2330 samples to 192 plot-date means. The plot structure is respected in the validation: whole replications are held out and inner folds are grouped by plot.

blocks.q: Why leave-one-replication-out and not random cross-validation?
blocks.a: Leaves of one plot share soil, micro-climate, variety and timing. Random splits would place leaves of the same plot in training and test and overestimate accuracy (Roberts et al., 2017). Holding out a whole replication tests the model as it would be used on a new replication.

blocks.q: The healthy plots were sprayed – is that a problem?
blocks.a: They provide true disease-free leaves of the same varieties and ages, which detection needs. They were rotated so that every test fold had four of them. For the covariate baseline they were excluded, because spraying, not the covariates, kept them healthy.

blocks.q: Why were the water bands kept?
blocks.a: The contact probe has its own lamp and touches the leaf, so there is no atmospheric water absorption, and the files were splice-corrected. These regions measure leaf water, which falls in diseased tissue; FD1245 and DWSI-2 come from them.

blocks.q: Why only first-derivative bands among the optimal wavelengths?
blocks.a: The derivative removes offsets between leaves and emphasises the red-edge shape, which changes with chlorophyll loss. SHAP and CARS both preferred derivatives, and the derivative correlates more strongly with grade (0.62) than reflectance (0.46).

blocks.q: Why did no band pair reach R² = 0.5?
blocks.a: Single leaves vary a lot within each grade (stage, date, leaf position), so two bands can explain at most about a third of the variation. The methodology foresaw this: the top 5% of pairs was used instead.

blocks.q: What is the White Rust Index and why is its third-band weight zero?
blocks.a: It adds a weighted third band to the best two-band index. For leaf spectra the best weight was zero: the third band did not improve the NIR-shoulder contrast. It may still help at canopy level, where background effects need correcting.

blocks.q: Why is six-grade accuracy so low?
blocks.a: Neighbouring grades overlap spectrally and visual grades are uncertain between neighbours. Most errors are one grade apart (75% within one grade, QWK 0.63). Detection and the severity score are the reliable outputs; for the UAV phase severity will be reported as a score or a few classes.

blocks.q: Is 83% detection accuracy good enough?
blocks.a: It was obtained on replications the model never saw, with balanced sensitivity and specificity and AUC 0.90. It is comparable to leaf-level results for other diseases and adequate for an early-warning layer; the decision threshold can be adjusted to the purpose (ROC curve).

blocks.q: Did DT-EDNet beat the other models?
blocks.a: No. At leaf level it reached 0.337 for six grades against 0.360 for ConvNeXt V2-Atto and 0.349 for RF, all within about one fold-to-fold SD. With 10–16 features the pseudo-images have no spatial structure; its strength is expected on the UAV hyperspectral images.

blocks.q: Why do the networks over-fit?
blocks.a: They have 0.95–11 million weights but only about 1000 training leaves after the validation split, and 10–16 inputs. They learn the useful pattern in a few epochs and then start memorising; early stopping on validation plots kept the best epoch.

blocks.q: How do you know there is no leakage?
blocks.a: All selection (band-pair maps, SHAP-CARS, ReliefF, VIF, SFFS) and all tuning were repeated inside each training part; the test replication was used once, only for the final metrics. Standardisation used training statistics only.

blocks.q: What does the covariate baseline show?
blocks.a: A model without sensor data (crop age, sowing date, variety, stage, weather) already explains much of the disease level. The spectra are credited only with the gain over it: +0.043 macro-F1 for six grades and +0.083 R² for the score, both confirmed with a plot-level bootstrap.

blocks.q: Then why are spectra worse than the covariates for detection?
blocks.a: Within the unsprayed plots almost all healthy leaves are from the first date, so the date alone separates them. A sensor survey does not know the sampling calendar, and with the sprayed healthy plots included the spectra detect disease with macro-F1 0.79 and AUC 0.90.

blocks.q: What do D1–D4 mean, and why did D4 have more disease at the same crop age?
blocks.a: Four sowing dates (9, 18, 27 December 2025 and 9 January 2026), i.e. crops of 50, 40, 30 and 20 days at the end of January. At equal crop age a later-sown crop is observed later in the season, when the epidemic had built up further, so the timing effect largely carries calendar time.

blocks.q: Why is the predicted score compressed towards the middle?
blocks.a: When the inputs explain only part of the variation (R² 0.46), a regression model hedges towards the mean: low grades are over-predicted and high grades under-predicted. The score ranks leaves correctly and can be calibrated before use as an absolute value.

blocks.q: Are the models specific to one variety or sowing date?
blocks.a: No. Trained on two varieties, a model performed as well on the third (macro-F1 0.34–0.39); trained on three sowing dates, it performed on the fourth (0.31–0.40), with RMSE close to the cross-validated value.

blocks.q: Why was the first date weaker in the strata?
blocks.a: On 11 February almost all leaves were grade 0–1, so there was little range of disease; grades are hard to separate and R² within that date is low.

blocks.q: Why was Objective 3 not addressed?
blocks.a: No pre-symptomatic dates were sampled in 2025-26: on the first date 45% of leaves already showed symptoms. The 2026-27 programme includes three pre-symptomatic UAV flights for this objective.

blocks.q: What will change in 2026-27?
blocks.a: UAV images with 13 flights (3 pre-symptomatic), plot and subplot features, multi-sensor fusion, the four severity classes plus disease-index regression, Objective 3, and external validation at Bharatpur.

blocks.q: Can these leaf models be applied directly to UAV images?
blocks.a: Not reliably: canopy pixels mix leaves, flowers, soil and shadow, and the illumination differs from the probe. The leaf results tell which wavelengths and features to use; the UAV models must be trained or calibrated on canopy data, with the leaf models used as a check.

blocks.q: How many models were compared, and which would you recommend?
blocks.a: Six machine-learning methods (SVM, RF, XGBoost, k-NN, PLS-DA/PLSR) and five networks. For detection SVM, for the score XGBoost or RF; for six grades the differences are within the noise, so a simple RF or SVM is preferred over a large network.

blocks.q: What is the single most important spectral indicator?
blocks.a: The red-edge position: it falls almost step by step from 709.0 nm (grade 0) to 701.3 nm (grade 9), was selected by ReliefF for every task and is among the most important SHAP features.

blocks.text: Appendix E. Glossary
**AUC.** Area under the ROC curve: probability that a diseased leaf gets a higher disease score than a healthy one (0.5 = chance, 1 = perfect).
**Balanced accuracy.** Average of sensitivity and specificity; not inflated by unequal class sizes.
**Bootstrap (plot-block).** Repeated resampling of whole plots with replacement to estimate the uncertainty of a metric or a gain.
**CARS.** Competitive adaptive reweighted sampling: repeatedly removes bands with small PLS coefficients and keeps the subset with the lowest error.
**Covariate baseline.** A model using only crop age, sowing date, variety, stage and weather – no spectra – against which the spectra are judged.
**DAS.** Days after sowing: crop age at sampling.
**DSF.** Disease-specific feature set: the 11 non-redundant bands and indices selected in Objective 1.
**DT-EDNet.** Dual transformer early-detection network of Ma et al. (2026), proposed for rice blast.
**Early stopping.** Stopping network training when the validation score stops improving, to avoid over-fitting.
**First derivative (FD).** The slope of the reflectance spectrum at each wavelength.
**Kappa.** Agreement beyond chance (0 = chance, 1 = perfect). Quadratic weighted kappa gives partial credit for near-misses on an ordered scale.
**Leakage.** Information from the test data entering model building, which inflates accuracy.
**LORO.** Leave-one-replication-out validation: train on two replications, test on the third.
**Macro-F1.** Average over classes of F1 (the harmonic mean of precision and recall); gives every class equal weight.
**NDSI / RSI.** Normalised difference and ratio of two bands.
**Over-fitting.** A model learning the training data too closely, including noise, so that it performs worse on new data.
**PCA.** Principal component analysis: summarises many correlated variables in a few uncorrelated components.
**Pseudo-image.** A vector of features arranged in a small square grid so that image networks can process it.
**Red edge, REP, Dr.** The steep rise of reflectance between about 680 and 760 nm; REP is the wavelength of its steepest point, Dr the height of the derivative there.
**ReliefF.** Feature ranking that rewards features separating nearby leaves of different classes.
**RMSE, MAE, R², RPD.** Root mean square error, mean absolute error, explained variance and ratio of the observed SD to RMSE.
**Savitzky–Golay.** A smoothing filter that fits a local polynomial in a moving window; it can also give derivatives.
**SFFS.** Sequential floating forward selection: adds features one by one, re-checking whether an earlier one can be removed.
**SHAP.** Shapley additive explanations: the contribution of each feature to each prediction.
**VIF.** Variance inflation factor: how much a feature is explained by the others (above 10 = strongly redundant).
Appendix F. Additional result tables
These tables give numbers that lie behind the figures but are not printed in the report. They are computed from the same pooled test predictions and data.

blocks.caption: Leaves by date: healthy block, unsprayed plots and grade counts.

parts: What it shows
The grade distribution on each date, and the share of healthy leaves among the unsprayed plots.
What we found
On 11 February, 46% of the unsprayed leaves were still healthy and none was grade 7 or 9.
On the later dates almost no unsprayed leaf was healthy (0–2.6%); healthy leaves then came only from the sprayed block.
Grade 9 leaves appeared from 24 February and were most frequent on 3 March (58).
What it means

This table explains the result of the covariate baseline for detection: inside the unsprayed plots, "healthy" almost means "11 February", so the date alone separates most healthy from diseased leaves.
Say to the chairman
"After the first date there were practically no healthy leaves in the unsprayed plots."

blocks.caption: Detection (SVM) by group.
Detection (SVM): sensitivity and specificity on each date.

parts: What it shows
How detection performed in each group and on each date.
What we found
Detection is stable across varieties, leaf positions and sowing timings (macro-F1 0.77–0.81).
On 11 February only half of the diseased leaves were found (sensitivity 0.50), while healthy leaves were recognised well (0.85).
From 24 February sensitivity was 0.84–0.89; specificity was lowest on 13 March (0.74).
What it means

Of the 94 diseased leaves missed on 11 February, 72 were grade 1 – very early symptoms with little spectral change. Detection becomes reliable once lesions are established. On 13 March, some healthy-block leaves were called diseased, possibly because ageing (senescence) produces spectral changes similar to disease.
Say to the chairman
"Very early, grade-1 leaves are hard to detect; once lesions develop, more than 85% of diseased leaves are found."

blocks.caption: Severity score (XGBoost) by group.

parts: What it shows
How the severity score performed in each group.
What we found
R² is 0.43–0.48 for varieties and timings, but lower within a single stage or date (0.28–0.40), and negative on 11 February.
The RMSE is smallest on 11 February (1.35) and in the vegetative stage (1.57), where the grades are low.
What it means

R² within a group is always lower than overall, because each group covers a narrower range of grades. On 11 February the leaves were almost all grade 0–1, so even a small error is large compared with the tiny spread of grades and R² becomes negative – the RMSE shows that the absolute error was actually the smallest.
Say to the chairman
"The score error is smallest early in the season; R² is low within a date only because the grades vary little within it."

blocks.caption: Size of the six-grade errors (share of the 2330 leaves).

parts: What it shows
How far off the six-grade predictions were.
What we found
About 39% of leaves were placed in the exact grade, about 74% within one grade, and only 8–10% three or more grade steps away.
What it means
Large errors are rare. The difference between the models lies mostly in the near-misses; for practical use the "within one grade" rate is the relevant number.
Say to the chairman
"Only about one leaf in eleven is badly misgraded."

blocks.caption: Severity score (XGBoost): mean prediction and error for each observed grade.

parts: What it shows
The prediction and error of the score model for each true grade.
What we found
Low grades are over-predicted by about 1.2–1.3 grade units; grade 7 is under-predicted by 2.1 and grade 9 by 3.7. The error is largest for grade 9 (RMSE 4.0).
What it means

This is the shrinkage seen in the predicted-versus-observed figure, in numbers. A simple calibration (stretching predictions back to the 0–9 range) could reduce the systematic part of the error, but it cannot remove the overlap between leaves; severe leaves will remain the hardest to quantify.
Say to the chairman
"The score under-estimates severe leaves – a grade-9 leaf is predicted at about 5 on average."

blocks.caption: Transfer tests (random forest): results on the held-out variety or sowing timing.

parts: What it shows
The complete results of the leave-one-variety-out and leave-one-timing-out tests.
What we found
Held-out varieties: macro-F1 0.34–0.39 and R² 0.45–0.53. Held-out timings: macro-F1 0.31–0.40 and R² 0.37–0.48.
What it means
The results on unseen groups match the cross-validated results (macro-F1 0.35, R² 0.45–0.46). The models do not depend on one variety or sowing date.
Say to the chairman
"On a variety or sowing date never seen in training the models perform as in cross-validation."

blocks.text: Appendix G. What each group of vegetation indices measures
The 44 published features of Table 13 fall into five groups. For each group, this appendix explains what it measures, how it responded to white rust in these data, and why.
Greenness and structure indices

parts: What it shows
**Members:** NDVI, NDVI850, SR, RVI, GNDVI, RDVI, MSR, OSAVI, TVI, MTVI2. They contrast near-infrared with red (or green) reflectance and respond to the amount of green tissue and leaf structure.
What we found
Moderate negative correlations (r −0.43 to −0.51) for the red-based indices; GNDVI was weak (−0.15) because green reflectance changed little.
What it means
Disease raises red and lowers NIR reflectance, so every NIR/red contrast falls. They are useful, but they also respond to leaf age and stage, so they are not specific to white rust.

blocks.text: Pigment indices

parts: What it shows
**Members:** PSSRa, PSSRb, PSSRc, SIPI, NPCI, PSRI, ARI, PRI, NPQI, MCARI, TCARI, VIgreen, GI. They target chlorophyll, carotenoids or anthocyanins through bands where each pigment absorbs.
What we found
PSSRb (−0.53) and ARI (+0.53) were among the strongest indices; PRI −0.46; MCARI, TCARI and PSSRc were weak (|r| ≤ 0.08).
What it means
Chlorophyll loss around the pustules lowers the chlorophyll-sensitive ratios; the rise of ARI and PSRI reflects the relative increase of other pigments in damaged and senescing tissue.

blocks.text: Red-edge indices and parameters

parts: What it shows
**Members:** CIrededge, NDRE, MTCI, REP, Dr, REarea. They describe the position, height and area of the red edge, which depend closely on chlorophyll content.
What we found
REP (−0.50), MTCI (−0.49), CIrededge and NDRE (−0.48 to −0.49), REarea (−0.48), Dr (−0.38).
What it means
The red edge shifts towards shorter wavelengths and flattens as chlorophyll is lost. REP was selected by ReliefF for every task and is the most regular single indicator.

blocks.text: Water indices

parts: What it shows
**Members:** WI, WBI, NDWI, MoistSI, NDII. They use the water absorption features near 970, 1240 and 1600 nm.
What we found
Moderate correlations (|r| 0.37–0.40): drier tissue in diseased leaves.
What it means
Infection damages cells and the tissue loses water, which raises reflectance in the water-sensitive bands. Their contribution is real but smaller than that of the red edge.

blocks.text: Disease and stress indices

parts: What it shows
**Members:** DWSI-1 to DWSI-5, HI, RVSI, RBI, NDBI. Indices proposed specifically for diseases (sugarcane rust, sugar-beet diseases, rice blast) that combine pigment, red-edge and water bands.
What we found
HI (−0.54) and RVSI (+0.56) were the strongest published indices overall; DWSI-2 was weakly correlated (+0.14) but carried independent information and entered the final feature set.
What it means

Indices designed for other leaf diseases transfer partly to white rust, because the underlying changes (chlorophyll loss, red-edge stress, water loss) are similar. DWSI-2 shows that a weak correlation alone does not make a feature useless.
